english_plan.summary_english: After describing God's seventh-day rest, the chapter recounts how the LORD God formed the man from dust, placed him in Eden, gave him a command, and made the woman as his corresponding helper. The man and woman live together without shame.

english_plan.summary_english: The flood destroys all breathing creatures on dry land outside the ark; only Noah, his family, and the animals with him survive.

english_plan.summary_english: The clans of Japheth, Ham, and Shem spread out into their lands, languages, and nations after the flood; among them Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD, begins his kingdom in Babylon and builds Nineveh, and from these clans the nations of the earth spread abroad.

english.original: Hebrew: שִׁנְעָר (Shinar), the plain of southern Mesopotamia
english.note: Genesis 10:10-12 names cities of Mesopotamia; several have been identified and excavated, while the exact location of Akkad remains uncertain. Babel is Babylon on the Euphrates; Erech is Uruk, one of the oldest cities in the world; Akkad gave its name to the Akkadian language that the whole Near East later used for diplomacy. Nineveh and Calah, both on the Tigris, became the capitals of Assyria, and the palace at Nineveh is where Sennacherib's wall reliefs were found. The verse traces the movement from the southern plain of Shinar northward to Assyria.

This translation reads Nimrod as the subject who went into Assyria and built Nineveh. Other translations read Asshur as that subject. Babel is Babylon and Erech is Uruk; the exact location of Akkad remains uncertain, so the cities in this list have not all been identified and excavated.

The numerical match compares a sale price with a sanctuary valuation; it does not establish a slave-market price schedule. Genesis 39:7-12: Potiphar's wife repeatedly solicits Joseph and seizes his cloak as he flees, locating those incidents in Genesis 39.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh; Aaron's staff becomes a snake and swallows the staffs of Pharaoh's magicians, but Pharaoh's heart hardens. english.note: Moses receives the command to instruct Aaron. Verse 20 identifies Aaron as the one who raises the staff and strikes the Nile.

english_plan.summary_english: God sends a plague killing Egyptian livestock in the field while sparing Israel's, then a plague of boils on people and animals; when Pharaoh still refuses to release Israel, God sends a devastating hailstorm that destroys crops and kills anyone caught outside, though it avoids Goshen. During the hail, Pharaoh promises to let Israel go, but after it stops he hardens his heart again and refuses.

english.note: The livestock warning in verse 3 specifies animals in the field. Later animals are brought under shelter before the hail. Pharaoh promises release while asking for the hail to stop, then hardens his heart after it stops.

refs_template.english: Exodus 8:15: Pharaoh hardens his heart after relief from a plague, establishing the earlier pattern repeated after the hail stops.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses warns Pharaoh of a locust plague; when it devastates Egypt, Pharaoh asks forgiveness, but after the locusts are blown away the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart again. The LORD then brings three days of darkness over Egypt, and when Pharaoh offers to let the Israelites go but retain their livestock, Moses refuses and Pharaoh orders him never to return.

english.note: This chapter names the LORD as the one who hardens Pharaoh's heart. Other passages describe Pharaoh hardening his own heart; the narrative uses both descriptions.

refs_template.english: Exodus 9:34: Pharaoh and his officials harden their hearts after the hail stops, supplying the self-hardening attribution alongside chapter 10's divine attribution.
Romans 9:17-18: Paul cites God's words to Pharaoh and speaks of God showing mercy and hardening, giving the later apostolic discussion of divine agency.

english_plan.summary_english: God commands Israel to consecrate the firstborn, redeem every firstborn son, and remember the exodus through the Feast of Unleavened Bread. He leads the people by cloud and fire, while Moses carries Joseph's bones as promised.

english.note: Every firstborn son must be redeemed, not sacrificed. The chapter distinguishes human redemption from the treatment of sacrificial animals, so consecration to the LORD cannot be read as permission for human sacrifice.

refs_template.english: Numbers 18:15-16: Firstborn sons must be redeemed for five shekels at one month old, explicitly distinguishing their consecration from sacrifice.
Luke 2:22-24: Jesus' parents present Him to the Lord and bring the prescribed birds, showing firstborn consecration within a family's observance of the law.
Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.

english_plan.summary_english: The chapter sets restitution for theft and property loss, and distinguishes bloodguilt in the killing of a burglar by night or after sunrise. It also gives laws on sexual conduct, sorcery, idolatry, loans, offerings, and protection of foreigners, widows, orphans, and the poor.

english.note: Verses 1-4 prescribe restitution for theft. The death in verses 2-3 is a burglar killed during a break-in, with different bloodguilt rules before and after sunrise; it is not a court's death sentence for stealing property.

refs_template.english: Leviticus 6:1-5: A person guilty of theft or deception must restore the property and add a fifth, providing a parallel law of restitution.
Job 24:16: Job describes thieves digging through houses in darkness, supplying the physical break-in setting relevant to the burglary law.

english_plan.summary_english: Nadab and Abihu die after offering unauthorized fire. Moses forbids Aaron and his remaining sons to perform the stated mourning rites or leave the tent, while Israel may mourn. The chapter gives priestly duties and records Moses accepting Aaron's explanation about the uneaten sin offering.

english.note: The restrictions name particular public mourning acts and departure from the tent. They do not say that Aaron felt no grief or was forbidden to grieve inwardly; verses 19-20 record his loss being taken seriously.

refs_template.english: Leviticus 21:1-12: Priests have specified family exceptions to corpse defilement, while the high priest faces stricter mourning and sanctuary restrictions, clarifying the ritual limits.

english_plan.summary_english: God instructs Moses and Aaron on which animals the Israelites may eat: land animals with divided hooves that chew cud, water creatures with fins and scales, permitted birds, and certain insects; all others are unclean, and touching their carcasses causes ceremonial uncleanness until evening.

english.note: The bird list names prohibited birds; it does not prohibit every bird. Deuteronomy 14:11 and 14:20 explicitly allow clean birds.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 14:11-20: The law expressly permits clean birds while listing prohibited birds, confirming that the dietary rules do not exclude every bird.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD gives distinct purification rules for abnormal discharges, emissions of semen, and menstruation. These include washing, periods of uncleanness, and, for specified abnormal discharges, offerings after seven clean days.

english.note: The chapter distinguishes ordinary semen emissions and menstruation from abnormal or prolonged discharges. The offerings after seven clean days belong to the specified abnormal discharges, not every bodily emission.

refs_template.english: Mark 5:25-34: Jesus heals a woman who has bled for twelve years, supplying a specific prolonged-bleeding case alongside Leviticus' distinct discharge rules.

english_plan.summary_english: The chapter assigns penalties for Molech worship and specified sexual and family offenses, and calls Israel to holiness. It distinguishes those who consult mediums, whom God will cut off, from mediums and spiritists themselves, who receive the stated death sentence.

english.original: Hebrew: אוֹב (ʾov) / יִדְּעֹנִי (yiddeʿoni), Greek: ἐγγαστρίμυθος (engastrimythos) / μάντις (mantis), Aramaic: אובא (ʾova) / ידעונא (yidʿona)
english.note: A medium or spiritist practices consultation of spirits or the dead. Verse 6 says God will cut off the consulter, while verse 27 assigns the stated death penalty to the medium or spiritist.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 18:9-14: The law forbids consulting mediums, spiritists, and the dead, providing the broader prohibition while Leviticus distinguishes the stated penalties.
1 Samuel 28:7-14: Saul consults a medium who fears being killed under his ban, and the narrative distinguishes the consulting king from the practitioner.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses is told to instruct Aaron and his sons that priests must be ceremonially clean to eat sacred offerings, and that only certain family members may consume them. God also specifies that sacrificial animals must be without defect, with a stated exception for certain freewill offerings, and gives rules about timing for young animals and thank offerings.

english.note: Verse 23 allows an ox or sheep with a deformed or stunted limb as a freewill offering, but not as fulfillment of a vow. The chapter's general requirement has this stated exception.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 23:21-23: A freely made vow must be fulfilled, while refraining from a vow incurs no guilt, clarifying the obligation behind a vow offering.

english_plan.summary_english: God instructs Moses on how to value dedicated persons, animals, houses, and land if someone makes a vow to the LORD, with specific redemption rules and prohibitions on substitution. Things irrevocably devoted to the LORD (cherem) follow separate rules and cannot be redeemed. Crop tithes may be redeemed by adding a fifth to their value; livestock tithes may not be redeemed or exchanged.

english.note: Monetary valuations for vows involving persons: fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty, thirty for a woman, twenty and ten for those aged five to twenty, five and three for children from one month to five years old, fifteen and ten for the elderly (27:3-7). At about 11.4 grams a shekel, fifty shekels is roughly 570 grams of silver. Verse 8 lets the priest set a lower figure for anyone who cannot pay.

Verses 2-8 assign monetary valuations for vows involving persons. Verses 28-29 treat cherem, irrevocable devotion, separately; they do not give a father permission to sentence an innocent child to death by a personal vow. Crop tithes may be redeemed with one fifth added, while livestock tithes may not.

refs_template.english: Judges 11:30-39: Jephthah vows a burnt offering, his only daughter greets him, and the account reports her mourning virginity and his fulfilling the vow.
Leviticus 5:4-6: A person who realizes guilt from a rash oath must confess and bring an offering for atonement, providing a remedy for rashly sworn words.
Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.

english_plan.summary_english: God instructs Moses to collect twelve staffs from the tribal leaders, place them in the tent of meeting, and declares that the staff of his chosen leader will sprout; the next day Aaron's staff has budded, blossomed, and produced almonds. Moses returns Aaron's staff to its place before the ark as a sign to silence the Israelites' complaints, though they respond with fear that they will die for approaching the tabernacle.

english.note: Numbers 17:10 places the staff before the Testimony. Hebrews 9:4 later lists Aaron's staff among the objects associated with the ark's contents; the two passages describe their settings differently.

refs_template.english: Hebrews 9:4: Hebrews lists Aaron's budded staff inside the ark, making its wording important alongside Numbers' description of placement before the Testimony.
Exodus 16:32-34: Aaron places a preserved jar of manna before the Testimony, providing parallel wording for the staff's placement in Numbers 17.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses and Eleazar count 601,730 men of military age and assign land by lot according to tribal size. The Levites are counted separately. Of the men counted in the first military census, only Caleb and Joshua remain.

english.note: The comparison concerns the men registered for military service, not every person alive at the exodus. The Levites have a separate count, and the children of the wilderness generation are the people now preparing to enter the land.

refs_template.english: Numbers 1:2-3: The first census registers men twenty or older who can serve in the army, defining the group compared with the later census.
Numbers 14:29-31: The counted adults are sentenced to die in the wilderness except Caleb and Joshua, while their children are promised entry into the land.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses gives laws on binding vows and the circumstances in which a father or husband may annul a woman's vow. The chapter also states that the vows of widows and divorced women are binding.

english.note: Verse 9 states that the vows of a widow or divorced woman are binding, without the father-or-husband annulment described elsewhere in the chapter. She is answerable to no father and no husband and her word is her own. Anna in Luke 2:36-37 is a widow living permanently at the temple in fasting and prayer, which is the kind of standing commitment this verse leaves open to her.

These rules address whether a vow is binding or can be annulled within a household. They do not turn a forbidden act into a lawful one. Leviticus 5:4-6 provides confession and atonement for rash oaths, and Deuteronomy 12:31 condemns child sacrifice.

Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses makes two new stone tablets, and God rewrites the Ten Commandments on the mountain; Moses then places the tablets in an acacia ark; he then recounts the Levites' assignment to carry the ark, rehearses God's demand for obedience and love, and reminds Israel of their growth from seventy ancestors to a nation as numerous as the stars.

english.note: Moses took the two new tablets up the mountain. After the LORD wrote the commandments and gave them back, Moses came down and put them in the ark.

refs_template.english: Exodus 34:1-4: Moses carries the two newly cut tablets up Mount Sinai for God to write on them, confirming that their placement in the ark comes later.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses warns against prophets, relatives, or towns that entice Israel to worship other gods. A town's guilt must be thoroughly established; its inhabitants are put to the sword, and the city and its plunder are burned and left in ruins.

english.note: Verses 14-16 require investigation and distinguish putting inhabitants to the sword from burning the city and its plunder. This is a specified judicial command about an idolatrous town, not permission for an individual to promise a child as a burnt offering.

refs_template.english: Exodus 22:20: Sacrificing to another god brings a sentence of devotion to destruction, giving the judicial idolatry context alongside Deuteronomy 13.
Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.

english_plan.summary_english: Moses gives restrictions on entry to the LORD's assembly, including people of illegitimate birth, Ammonites, and Moabites, and specifies when Edomite and Egyptian descendants may enter. He also gives laws on camp purity, refugees, lending, vows, and neighboring fields.

english.note: The Hebrew birth-status term is rendered differently in English translations, including illegitimate birth or birth from an unlawful union. This legal restriction is not a statement that a child personally committed the parents' sin. Ruth and Isaiah 56 are important context for the chapter's language about descent and belonging.

refs_template.english: Ruth 4:13-17: Ruth marries Boaz and bears Obed, David's grandfather, supplying a family-history passage to read alongside the descent restrictions.
Isaiah 56:3-7: The LORD promises covenant-keeping eunuchs and foreigners a place in His house and accepted worship, supplying context for assembly restrictions.
Acts 8:26-39: Philip explains the good news about Jesus to an Ethiopian eunuch and baptizes him, providing a later account of a eunuch's reception.

english_plan.summary_english: Joshua defeats the northern alliance at Merom, destroys Hazor, and captures its allied cities. He removes the Anakim from Israel's hill country, while some remain in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The chapter closes with the land allotted to Israel and rest from war.

english.note: Verse 22 explicitly leaves Anakim in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. The conquest summary must be read alongside that limit and the later account of territory still remaining, rather than as the extinction of every Anakite.

refs_template.english: Numbers 13:28-33: The spies report fortified cities and descendants of Anak, identifying the people discussed in Joshua's later conquest account.
1 Samuel 17:4: Goliath comes from Gath, one of the cities named in Joshua 11's qualification about surviving Anakim.
Joshua 13:1-6: The LORD tells the aged Joshua that much territory remains unpossessed, including Philistine cities, qualifying an unrestricted reading of conquest summaries.

english_plan.summary_english: The remaining tribes receive their allotted territories: Simeon within Judah's borders, followed by Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with specified town lists and boundaries for each. Joshua is then given Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, completing the land division overseen by Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh.

english.note: Simeon's inheritance lay inside Judah's territory. The tribes assigned in this chapter were not all in the north.

refs_template.english: Joshua 15:20-32: Judah's southernmost towns are listed in the Negev, establishing the southern geography of the territory within which Simeon receives towns.

english_plan.summary_english: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bokim for breaking covenant and disobeying his commands; after Joshua's death, a new generation abandons the LORD for foreign gods, prompting him to give them over to raiders and establish a cycle where judges save them temporarily but they return to idolatry after each judge dies.

english.note: The Hebrew shofet can describe a ruler or someone who gives judgment. In Judges, God raises deliverers against Israel's oppressors, but their role is not limited to warfare. Deborah is both a prophet and a judge; Israelites come to her for judgment (4:4-5). The title therefore includes judicial authority as well as leadership and deliverance.

refs_template.english: Judges 4:4-5: Deborah is both a prophet and a judge, and Israelites come to her for judgment, showing that the judges' role includes judicial decisions.
Deuteronomy 16:18-20: Israel must appoint judges who judge fairly, reject bribes, and pursue justice, establishing the judicial function associated with the title.

english_plan.summary_english: Gideon appeases Ephraim, defeats the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, and punishes Succoth and Penuel for refusing aid. He refuses kingship but makes a gold ephod and places it in Ophrah; Israel worships the ephod, which becomes a snare to Gideon and his household. After his death, Israel turns to the Baals and forgets the LORD's deliverance.

english.note: Exodus 28 describes the high priest's ephod as a garment associated with the breastpiece of judgment. Judges 8:27 uses the same word for the object Gideon made and placed in Ophrah, but does not describe its exact shape or say whether it was wearable. Verse 26 weighs the collected earrings at 1,700 shekels; the account does not explain how that gold was incorporated. Israel's idolatrous attachment is to the ephod. It becomes a snare to Gideon and his household; Gideon himself is not described as becoming an idol. The prescribed garment uses gold, blue, purple, and scarlet, with shoulder pieces and a woven band; the breastpiece containing the Urim and Thummim is fastened to it (Exodus 28:6-30). In 1 Samuel 23:9-12, David calls for the ephod when inquiring of the LORD.

refs_template.english: Exodus 28:6-30: The prescribed priestly ephod is a woven garment associated with Aaron's breastpiece of judgment, providing the priestly background for the object named in Gideon's story.
Judges 9:1-6: Abimelech massacres his brothers, Jotham escapes, and the men of Shechem make Abimelech king, beginning the aftermath of Gideon's household.
Judges 17:5: Micah makes an ephod and household idols for his private shrine and appoints his son as priest, another use of an ephod within the book's accounts of unauthorized worship.
Judges 18:17-20: The Danites take Micah's ephod along with his images, and his priest gladly joins them, continuing the story of religious objects diverted into private and tribal worship.

english_plan.summary_english: Abimelech murders his brothers to become king of Shechem; Jotham escapes and pronounces a curse on Abimelech and the city. After three years, conflict erupts and Abimelech destroys Shechem and its tower. At Thebez a woman crushes his skull with a millstone; at his request, his armor-bearer then kills him with a sword.

english.original: Hebrew: אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Abimelek), my father is king
english.note: Verse 5 describes a dynastic massacre of Abimelech's brothers on one stone, but explicitly says that Jotham, the youngest, escaped. Abimelech's own name means my father is king, which is what Gideon had refused to be (8:23), and his claim rests on his mother's family at Shechem rather than his father's house at Ophrah. Jehu does the same thing to Ahab's seventy sons at Samaria, and has their heads sent to him in baskets (2 Kings 10:1-8).

Jotham escapes the massacre of Gideon's sons (9:5). At Thebez, a woman's millstone crushes Abimelech's skull, and his armor-bearer then kills him with a sword at his request (9:53-54). Both the woman's blow and the armor-bearer's action belong to the account of his death.

refs_template.english: 2 Samuel 11:21: Abimelech's death at Thebez from a woman's upper millstone is recalled as a warning about approaching a wall, preserving the memory of the woman's decisive blow.

english_plan.summary_english: Tola judges Israel for twenty-three years and Jair for twenty-two. Israel again serves foreign gods, and the LORD gives them over to Philistine and Ammonite oppression; the Ammonites oppress the Israelites in Gilead for eighteen years. Israel repents and removes its idols, and Gilead's leaders promise leadership to whoever begins the fight against Ammon.

english.note: Ammon descended from Lot through his younger daughter, which is what Genesis 19:38 records, so Israel and Ammon were reckoned distant kin. Their country lay east of the Jordan on the desert edge, with its capital at Rabbah, the site of modern Amman. 1 Kings 11:5 names Milcom as the Ammonite god; 11:7 and 2 Kings 23:10 name Molech, with the latter passage condemning the burning of children as offerings. Verse 8 describes eighteen years of oppression in Gilead east of the Jordan; verse 9 then reports the Ammonites crossing the river to attack Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim.

The chapter gives Tola twenty-three years and Jair twenty-two (10:2-3). It names both Philistine and Ammonite oppressors, but the eighteen years in verse 8 refer to the oppression of Israelites east of the Jordan in Gilead. Verse 9 then reports the Ammonites crossing the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim.

english_plan.summary_english: Gilead makes Jephthah its leader, and he disputes Ammon's claim to Israel's land. Before fighting, he vows to offer as a burnt offering whatever comes out of his house to meet him if the LORD grants victory. He defeats Ammon, but his only child, his daughter, comes out to greet him. After two months mourning her virginity, she returns, and he does to her as he vowed. The narrator adds that she had never known a man. Israel's daughters lament her for four days each year.

english.note: Olah in verse 31 means a burnt offering. Verse 39 reports that Jephthah did to his daughter as he had vowed; together, these statements strongly support literal sacrifice, although the killing is not separately described. Her virginity is consistent with death before marriage and motherhood; she was his only child. The lifelong-dedication reading is a less direct alternative: some interpreters read the two clauses in verse 31 as dedication or sacrifice, but that distinction is disputed, and verse 39 does not state a subsequent life of celibacy. The Torah condemns child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10; Leviticus 18:21). A vow cannot authorize it, and recording an act does not establish God's approval. The Spirit comes upon Jephthah before his vow (11:29-30). Leviticus 5:4-6 provides confession and atonement for sinful rash oaths. Leviticus 27:1-8 concerns monetary valuations; cherem in 27:28-29 is distinct and does not authorize a father to kill an innocent daughter through a personal vow.

refs_template.english: Leviticus 27:1-8: Special vows involving persons carry monetary valuations, and a priest adjusts the amount for someone too poor to pay, distinguishing these rules from instructions to sacrifice a person.

Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not worship the LORD through practices such as burning sons and daughters as sacrifices, explicitly prohibiting the kind of act a personal vow might be invoked to excuse.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is stopped before killing Isaac and offers a ram in his place, contrasting God's intervention here with the vow and its reported fulfillment in Judges 11.
Deuteronomy 18:10: No one in Israel may sacrifice a son or daughter in the fire, establishing a prohibition that Jephthah's vow cannot override.
Leviticus 18:21: Giving children as sacrifices to Molech is forbidden as profaning God's name, another explicit Torah prohibition of child sacrifice.
Leviticus 5:4-6: Guilt from a thoughtless oath calls for confession and a sin offering through which the priest makes atonement, providing the Torah's response to sinful rash sworn speech.

Leviticus 27:28-29: Devoted things cannot be sold or redeemed, and a person devoted to destruction cannot be ransomed but must be put to death; this concerns cherem, a distinct category from the vow recorded in Judges 11.
Leviticus 1:3-9: A burnt offering from the herd is slaughtered, cut into pieces, and burned on the altar, establishing the sacrificial meaning of the offering named in Jephthah's vow.

english_plan.summary_english: Ephraim confronts Jephthah over the Ammonite war, and Gilead defeats Ephraim. At the Jordan fords, Gileadite guards use 'Shibboleth' to identify and kill fleeing Ephraimites; the chapter reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed at that time. Jephthah judges Israel for six years, followed by Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.

english.note: Shibbolet can mean an ear of grain or a flowing stream; the test in this account depends on its pronunciation. The guards use Shibboleth to identify fleeing Ephraimites at the Jordan crossings. The chapter reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed 'at that time' after describing both the battle and the ford killings (12:4-6). It gives no separate battle and ford totals. The summary should retain the reported count without assigning every death to the pronunciation test.

refs_template.english: Judges 8:1-3: An earlier quarrel over exclusion from battle ends when Gideon's reply calms Ephraim, contrasting with the fighting between Ephraim and Gilead in Judges 12.
Proverbs 15:1: A gentle answer turns away anger, while harsh speech stirs it up, providing a wisdom parallel to the contrasting responses to Ephraim in Judges 8 and 12.

english_plan.summary_english: The angel of the LORD promises Manoah's childless wife a son, a Nazirite to God from the womb, who will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Manoah offers a sacrifice to the LORD, and the angel ascends in its flame. The woman later gives birth to Samson, whom the LORD blesses.

english.note: The announcement says Samson will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines (13:5); it does not promise that he will complete their liberation. His dedication begins in the womb and lasts for life. Numbers 6 also describes voluntary Nazirite vows that end after a stated period with offerings and the shaving of the head. Samson's lifelong calling is therefore distinct from that ordinary pattern.

refs_template.english: Numbers 6:1-21: Nazirite separation includes uncut hair, restrictions on grape products and corpse contact, and offerings and shaving when the period ends, supplying the legal background for Samson's dedication.

1 Samuel 7:7-14: The LORD answers Samuel against the Philistines, Israel recovers territory, and Philistine attacks cease during Samuel's days, showing a later stage of the deliverance Samson was to begin.

english_plan.summary_english: Samson insists on marrying a Philistine woman, while the narrator says the LORD is seeking an occasion against Philistine rule. At the wedding feast, the Philistine companions threaten to burn his wife and her father's household unless she obtains the riddle's answer. Under that threat she presses Samson, and he tells her. After the answer is disclosed, the Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson; he kills thirty men in Ashkelon and takes their clothes to pay the wager. His wife is then given to his companion.

english.term: The lion's carcass and the Nazirite rule
english.note: Verses 8 and 9 have Samson turn aside to the dead lion, take honey from it, eat it, and give some to his parents without telling them where it came from. Leviticus 11:24-28 addresses uncleanness from animal carcasses. Numbers 6:6-7 addresses corpse contact for Nazirites and specifically names parents and siblings; applying that rule directly to this lion requires interpretation.

The Philistine companions threaten to burn Samson's wife and her father's household unless she obtains the riddle's answer (14:15). Her pressure on Samson occurs under that threat. Verse 4 separately explains the LORD's purpose in creating an occasion against Philistine rule; that larger purpose does not make every character's conduct a command from God. Leviticus 11:24-28 addresses animal-carcass uncleanness. Numbers 6:6-7 addresses corpse contact for Nazirites and specifically mentions parents and siblings; applying that passage directly to the lion requires interpretation.

refs_template.english: Judges 15:6: The Philistines burn Samson's wife and her father to death, showing that the threatened violence in the wedding story later reaches both of them.

english_plan.summary_english: Samson finds that his wife has been given to his companion and burns the Philistines' crops. The Philistines burn his wife and her father, and Samson retaliates with a great slaughter. Judah binds him and hands him over, but the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break free and kill a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone. When he cries out in thirst, God provides water.

english.original: Hebrew: לֶחִי (Lechi) - Hebrew: עֵין הַקּוֹרֵא (Ein ha-Qore)
english.note: Lehi is already named in verse 9, while Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore receive explicit naming explanations later in the chapter. Lehi means jawbone, Ramath-lehi means the height of the jawbone, and En-hakkore means the spring of the one who called. The pattern of naming a place after what happened there runs through the whole Old Testament, and it is how a landscape kept its history when almost nobody could read.

The Philistines burn both Samson's wife and her father (15:6). Samson and the men of Judah give their own explanations for the cycle of retaliation, while the narrator separately reports the Spirit's empowerment and God's provision of water. The place-name explanations also differ: Lehi is already named in verse 9; Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore receive explicit naming explanations later in the chapter.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 32:35: The LORD claims vengeance and repayment as His own, providing a point of comparison for Samson's personal declarations of retaliation.
Exodus 22:6: The person whose fire consumes stacked or standing grain or a field must make restitution, supplying legal background for the destruction of the Philistines' crops.

english_plan.summary_english: Samson carries away Gaza's gates and later tells Delilah that his uncut hair marks his dedication to God as a Nazirite. After his hair is shaved, his strength leaves him; the narrator says the LORD has departed from him. The Philistines blind and imprison him. He later prays for strength and brings down their temple, dying with thousands of Philistines.

english.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר הָעִיר (shaar ha-ir), the city gate
english.note: Gaza was the southernmost of the five Philistine cities, on the coast road running down to Egypt. The gate was the single heaviest and most valuable piece of a town's defence: two leaves of timber plated or braced, hung on posts sunk into the ground, with a bar dropped across at dusk. Verse 3 has Samson pull out the doors, both posts and the bar together and carry them to a hill facing Hebron; the verse gives no travel distance or elevation gain. The town wakes up with no gate.

Samson identifies his uncut hair with his dedication to God as a Nazirite (16:17). After the shaving, the narrator explains that the LORD had departed from him (16:20); the account does not present hair as an independent source of power. Verse 3 places the hill in relation to Hebron but gives neither a travel distance nor an elevation gain. Those numerical estimates depend on identifying the hill geographically.

refs_template.english: Judges 13:5: Samson is designated a Nazirite to God from the womb, and no razor is to touch his head, connecting his uncut hair with his consecration.
Numbers 6:5: Uncut hair belongs to a Nazirite's vowed separation to the LORD, supplying the legal background for Samson's explanation of his hair.

english_plan.summary_english: Micah returns stolen silver to his mother, who dedicates it to the LORD but uses part to make an idol. Micah makes a private shrine and hires a wandering Levite as his priest, then assumes the LORD will prosper him. The narrator frames the period as one in which everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

english.note: The tribe of Levi got no territory. It was given forty-eight towns scattered through the other tribes, and it lived on the tithes and the offerings brought to the sanctuary (Numbers 18:21-24, Joshua 21:41). Deuteronomy 18:6-8 gives a Levite the right to leave his town, come to the place the LORD chooses, and serve there on equal terms. Verses 7 to 13 describe a young Levite from Bethlehem looking for somewhere to live and accepting wages as a private household priest; the chapter does not state that the national support system had stopped working.

Verse 10 sets the Levite's terms: ten shekels of silver a year, a suit of clothes, and his food. That is about four ounces of silver annually, and it is one of the few plain wage figures in the Old Testament, useful for reading every other price in Scripture.

Micah's mother dedicates the silver to the LORD while using it for an image; Micah assumes that hiring a Levite guarantees the LORD's favor (17:3-5,13). The chapter reports these actions and Micah's belief without endorsing them. Levite status alone does not confer Aaronic priesthood (Numbers 3:5-10). The chapter reports the Levite accepting wages, clothing, and food; it does not identify a collapse of the national tithe system as the reason for his choice.

refs_template.english: Exodus 20:4-6: Making and worshiping images is forbidden, so dedicating Micah's silver to the LORD does not authorize the images made from it.
Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites are assigned to assist Aaron and his sons, while Aaron and his sons receive the priestly duties, distinguishing Levite status from appointment to the priesthood.
Deuteronomy 18:1-8: Levites receive designated support and may come to minister at the place the LORD chooses, supplying the lawful setting for their service alongside Micah's private arrangement.

english_plan.summary_english: Danite spies scout Laish, and six hundred armed Danites march there. They steal Micah's religious objects, and his priest gladly joins them after being offered a position with the tribe. They threaten Micah, destroy unsuspecting Laish, rebuild it as Dan, and establish idol worship there.

english.note: The Danites steal Micah's religious objects, but the priest gladly accepts their offer to serve the tribe rather than one household (18:19-20). Verse 30 has a textual difference: some witnesses read Moses, while many Hebrew manuscripts indicate Manasseh with a raised letter nun. Editions differ accordingly. The Hebrew word translated son can also express descent, as reflected in translations using descendant. The genealogy connects the shrine's priesthood with an Israelite family; the textual and generational details require care. Exodus 2:22 and 18:3 name Moses' son Gershom. Judges 18:30 names Jonathan and says his descendants served as priests for the Danites until the captivity of the land.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 12:5-7: Israel is to bring sacrifices and vow offerings to the place the LORD chooses, contrasting with the Danites' establishment of worship around Micah's stolen images.
Exodus 2:22: Moses names his son Gershom, supplying the family background for the Moses reading in the genealogy of the Danite priest.

english_plan.summary_english: A Levite brings his concubine back from her father's house in Bethlehem. At Gibeah, a mob demands to abuse him. The host offers the women instead, and the Levite seizes his concubine and puts her outside. The men rape and abuse her through the night. In the morning she lies unresponsive at the doorway; the Levite takes her home, cuts her into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel.

english.note: The Hebrew wording of 19:2 is rendered unfaithful in some editions; ancient witnesses and other translations support angry. The difference concerns how the woman came to be at her father's house. In verse 25, the Levite seizes her and puts her outside to the mob. The narrator then describes the night's abuse, her collapse at the doorway, and her failure to respond in the morning. The passage does not explicitly state the exact moment of her death. The Levite later says that she died in his account to the assembly (20:5).

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 22:25-27: The law condemns the man who overpowers a betrothed woman and expressly clears her of guilt, providing a legal contrast to blaming a woman for being attacked.
Judges 20:4-6: In his report to the assembly, the Levite says the attackers meant to kill him and that his concubine died, providing his own account to compare with chapter 19's narration.
Genesis 19:4-11: Sodom's mob demands Lot's guests, and Lot offers his daughters instead before the visitors intervene, paralleling the threat and proposed substitution at Gibeah.

english_plan.summary_english: Israel assembles at Mizpah and hears the Levite's account of the atrocity at Gibeah. Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men. After two costly defeats, Israel defeats Benjamin using an ambush and burns its towns. Six hundred Benjaminite men escape to the rock of Rimmon.

english.note: Verse 47 has six hundred Benjaminites hold out four months on a rock in the wilderness east of the hill country. Sela means a crag or cliff, not a boulder, and country like that is full of limestone spurs with caves and one approach, which is why fugitives head for them all through Scripture; David does the same at Adullam and En-gedi. These are the six hundred male survivors named at the chapter's close; chapter 21 addresses the separate crisis over wives after the destruction of Benjamin's women.

Verses 4-6 record the Levite's own speech. His account omits his role in putting the woman outside and presents the mob's intent differently from 19:22-25. The assembly acts on that testimony, while the reader has also heard the preceding narrator. The war's final devastation extends to Benjamin's towns and those found there (20:48). The six hundred who escape to Rimmon are explicitly men; chapter 21 then addresses the loss of Benjamin's women.

refs_template.english: Judges 19:22-30: The narrator describes a demand to abuse the male guest and the Levite putting the woman outside, details that differ from or disappear in his later speech to the assembly.
Judges 21:16: The elders say Benjamin's women have been destroyed, explaining why the surviving Benjaminites face a separate crisis over wives.

english_plan.summary_english: Israel grieves for Benjamin but seeks to work around its oaths through further violence. The assembly destroys Jabesh-gilead and gives four hundred spared young women to the surviving Benjaminites. When that is insufficient, the elders arrange for Benjaminites to abduct women dancing at Shiloh. The book closes with everyone doing what was right in his own eyes.

english.note: The women from Jabesh-gilead are captives spared from an attack that kills the town's other inhabitants (21:10-12). The women at Shiloh are abducted under a plan arranged by Israel's elders (21:20-23). These are the assembly's decisions, not commands from God. Numbers 30:2 requires truthful fulfillment of vows and oaths, while Leviticus 5:4-6 provides confession and atonement for sinful rash speech. An oath does not authorize wrongdoing. The book's closing statement about everyone doing what was right in his own eyes frames the outcome. The assembly had sworn not to give daughters to Benjaminites (21:1) and to put to death anyone who failed to attend the gathering (21:5).

refs_template.english: Leviticus 5:4-6: Guilt from rash sworn speech calls for confession and a sin offering for atonement, relevant when Israel's own oaths become the reason given for further violence.
1 Samuel 14:24-45: Saul demands Jonathan's death after Jonathan unknowingly violates his food oath, but the people rescue Jonathan, another account of a leader's oath placing a child under threat.

english_plan.summary_english: Samuel vindicated his leadership before all Israel, then recounted God's faithfulness through the judges before warning that blessing depends on both the people and the new king obeying the LORD. When the people fear the thunder and rain Samuel called down, he reassures them that the LORD will not abandon His people for the sake of His great name, and calls them to serve Him faithfully.

english.note: The command applies to the people and their king together. Verse 14 requires both to follow the LORD; it does not put the king beside God as a separate object of this obedience. In verse 22, the stated reason that the LORD will not abandon His people is His great name and His choice to make them His own. Verses 24-25 call for faithful service and warn against persisting in wickedness; they should not be substituted for the reason given in verse 22.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 17:18-20: Israel's king must copy, read, and obey God's law, confirming that the king is also subject to the LORD's commands.

english_plan.summary_english: Jonathan's attack brings a Philistine mobilization that terrifies Israel. Saul waits seven days at Gilgal but offers the burnt offering before Samuel arrives as his army disperses. Samuel rebukes his disobedience and says his dynasty will not endure.

english.note: Saul did wait seven days. The disputed action comes when he offers before Samuel arrives, explaining that the army was scattering and the Philistines threatened him. Samuel calls it disobedience to the LORD's command.

refs_template.english: 1 Samuel 10:8: Samuel tells Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal until he comes, supplying the instruction behind the later rebuke.

english_plan.summary_english: Jonathan makes a covenant with David, whose success makes Saul jealous. Saul tries to kill him and sets a dangerous bride-price for Michal, hoping the Philistines will kill him. David exceeds the required price and marries Michal.

english.note: The price was a trap, not an impossible condition: Saul hoped David would die while collecting one hundred Philistine foreskins. David returned with two hundred. The chapter also says Michal loved David.

refs_template.english: 2 Samuel 9:1-7: David seeks Jonathan's surviving son and promises restored land and a place at his table, showing the later expression of their covenant loyalty.

english_plan.summary_english: David seeks a survivor of Saul's house to show kindness for Jonathan's sake. He brings Mephibosheth from Machir's house at Lo-debar, restores Saul's land to him, and gives him a permanent place at the royal table.

english.note: Second Samuel 4:4 explains the injury: Mephibosheth was five when the news came from Jezreel, his nurse picked him up and fled, and he fell and became lame in both feet. Verse 13 says he lived in Jerusalem and ate at the king's table, and again states that he was lame in both feet. In 19:26 he says he intended to travel on a donkey.

Verse 4 finds Jonathan's son living at Lo-debar in Gilead, east of the Jordan, in the household of Machir son of Ammiel. Machir turns up once more, sending food and bedding to David at Mahanaim when Absalom drives him out (17:27-29), so the man who housed Saul's grandson later supplies David's army.

Verses 7, 10, 11, and 13 repeat that Mephibosheth eats at the king's table. A place at the table was a formal grant of maintenance for life at royal expense, recorded the same way for the released Jehoiachin in Babylon (2 Kings 25:29).
Mephibosheth is living in Machir's house at Lo-debar. The chapter does not say he is hiding or explain why he lives there. Machir later supplies David during Absalom's rebellion.

refs_template.english: 1 Samuel 20:14-17: Jonathan asks David to preserve loving devotion toward his household, establishing the covenant obligation behind David's kindness to Mephibosheth.
2 Samuel 17:27-29: Machir of Lo-debar helps supply David and his people at Mahanaim, confirming his later connection with David without explaining Mephibosheth's earlier residence.

english_plan.summary_english: Nathan confronts David over Bathsheba and Uriah. David confesses, the child dies despite his prayer, and Solomon is later born. At Rabbah, Joab captures the water supply and calls David to complete the conquest; David takes the crown and plunder and puts the people to work.

english.note: The Hebrew word behind repent is not about feeling; it is the ordinary verb for turning round and going back, used of a traveller or an army. What the prophets ask for is a change of direction that can be seen from outside. This chapter shows the difference between remorse and repentance in David's response: verses 16 to 20 have David fasting and lying on the ground for seven days over the child, then washing, anointing himself and going in to worship the moment the child dies.

Joab reports taking the water supply and asks David to bring the remaining troops and take the city. David then captures it. The account distinguishes Joab's siege success from David's final capture. The English Berean Standard Bible renders 12:31 as forced labor with tools and brickmaking; other editions describe killing the captives with tools. The wording is interpreted differently, so this treatment needs to be distinguished from the account of who captured the city. 1 Chronicles 20:3 is the parallel account.

refs_template.english: 1 Chronicles 20:1-3: The parallel account assigns Rabbah's siege to Joab and the crown, plunder, and labor arrangements to David, distinguishing their actions.

english_plan.summary_english: David organizes his forces into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, then positions himself at the city gate while his troops march out; Absalom's head is caught in an oak tree during the battle; despite David's command to spare him, Joab thrusts three spears into him and ten armor-bearers kill him. Runners bring word to David that the battle is won, but when he learns Absalom is dead, he grieves deeply in the gateway chamber, lamenting that he wishes he had died instead of his son.

english.note: Verse 9 says Absalom's head was caught in the tree; it does not identify his hair as the cause. Joab thrust three spears into him, and ten armor-bearers then struck and killed him.

refs_template.english: 2 Samuel 14:25-26: Absalom's appearance and unusually heavy hair are described, supplying the earlier detail often connected with the later tree episode.

english_plan.summary_english: A three-year famine is linked to Saul's attack on the Gibeonites. David hands seven of Saul's descendants over to the Gibeonites, who execute them; after the remains are buried, God answers prayer for the land. David's forces also defeat several Philistine giants.

english.term: The Gibeonites and the broken oath
english.note: Verses 1 and 2 reach back nearly four centuries. The Gibeonites had obtained a treaty from Joshua by deception, and Israel swore to them by the LORD and kept it even after the fraud came out (Joshua 9:15-20). Saul broke that oath and tried to wipe them out, and the famine is laid at that. Verse 4 records their refusal of silver or gold. They ask for seven descendants of Saul, whom David hands over for execution; the chapter does not identify each victim's personal involvement in Saul's attack. Numbers 35:31 forbids accepting a ransom for a murderer who is guilty and deserves death.

The famine is connected with Saul's attack on the Gibeonites, whose treaty Israel had sworn to honor. David hands over seven descendants of Saul; the Gibeonites execute them. The chapter does not identify each victim's personal involvement in Saul's attack, and Deuteronomy 24:16 prohibits executing children for their fathers' sins.

refs_template.english: Joshua 9:15-20: Israel's leaders preserve their sworn treaty with the Gibeonites after discovering the deception, establishing the oath behind the later bloodguilt dispute.
Deuteronomy 24:16: Parents and children must not be executed for one another's sins, supplying the law relevant to the execution of Saul's descendants.

english_plan.summary_english: The chapter presents David's final oracle about just rule, God's covenant, and judgment on evil. It then lists his mighty warriors and their exploits, ending with thirty-seven men in all.

english.note: Verses 1-7 present David's oracle. The list of his mighty men begins at verse 8; the chapter does not say David compiled or recited that list as part of the oracle.

refs_template.english: 1 Chronicles 11:10-47: Chronicles separately lists David's mighty men and their exploits, providing the parallel catalog to the list following his last oracle.

english_plan.summary_english: In anger against Israel, the LORD incites David to order a census. David later confesses sin, and a plague kills seventy thousand before the LORD stops it. David buys Araunah's threshing floor and offers sacrifices, and God answers prayer for the land.

english.original: Hebrew: כֹּפֶר נֶפֶשׁ (kopher nephesh), a ransom for a life
english.note: Samuel opens with the LORD's anger against Israel and says He incited David; Chronicles names Satan as the inciter. David confesses that the census was sinful. Exodus 30 connects a census ransom with protection from plague, but neither account explicitly says David omitted that payment or gives that as the sole explanation. Exodus 30:11-16 sets the census ransom at half a shekel for each counted man, rich and poor alike, to support the Tent of Meeting.

refs_template.english: Exodus 30:11-16: A census requires a half-shekel ransom from each counted man to prevent plague, supplying the relevant law without proving what David omitted.
1 Chronicles 21:1-8: The parallel account names Satan as the census inciter and records David's confession, preserving its different attribution from Samuel.

english_plan.summary_english: Solomon builds his palace over thirteen years and commissions Huram of Tyre to make the temple's bronze furnishings. The chapter also records the gold sanctuary furnishings made for Solomon's temple.

english.note: The chapter names Huram as the skilled bronze craftsman. Its statement that Solomon made the gold furnishings credits the king with the work; it does not describe him personally shaping the metal.

refs_template.english: 2 Chronicles 4:11-22: Huram's bronze craftsmanship and furnishings credited to Solomon appear together, providing the parallel account of the temple work.

english_plan.summary_english: Ahab covets Naboth's vineyard; when Naboth refuses, Jezebel orchestrates his execution through false testimony and has him stoned to death. Elijah confronts Ahab with God's judgment - his line will be destroyed and dogs will lick his blood - but when Ahab humbles himself in sackcloth, God delays the disaster until his son's time.

english.note: Elijah predicts that dogs will lick Ahab's blood. The prediction that dogs will devour a body concerns Jezebel. The later accounts preserve that distinction.

refs_template.english: 1 Kings 22:37-38: Dogs lick Ahab's blood when his chariot is washed after his death, recording the fulfillment concerning his blood.
2 Kings 9:30-37: Eunuchs throw Jezebel down at Jehu's command and her remains are largely consumed, with Jehu citing Elijah's prediction about dogs eating her flesh.

english_plan.summary_english: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind as a chariot of fire separates him from Elisha after crossing the Jordan; Elisha inherits his cloak and spirit, heals bad water in Jericho with salt, and curses youths who mock him, resulting in bears mauling forty-two of them.

english.note: The chariot and horses of fire separate the two prophets. Verse 11 says that Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind; it does not say he rode the chariot.

english_plan.summary_english: Joram of Israel, with Judah and Edom's help, campaigns against rebellious Moab; Elisha promises water and victory, the armies prevail, and the Moabites are defeated and their land ravaged. Moab's king then sacrifices his firstborn son on the wall; great fury comes against Israel, and the allies withdraw.

english.note: Chemosh was the national god of Moab; Numbers 21:29 calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh, and Solomon built him a high place east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7). Verse 27 reports Mesha taking his oldest son, the heir to his throne, and burning him as an offering on the city wall in full view of the besieging armies. The account then reports great fury against Israel and the allies' withdrawal; it does not identify the source of the fury or explicitly name the recipient of the offering.

The last verse reports the king sacrificing his firstborn, great fury against Israel, and the allies' withdrawal. It does not identify the source of that fury or explicitly name the recipient of the offering. The account records the act; it does not command or approve it.

refs_template.english: Leviticus 18:21: The law forbids giving children as sacrifices to Molech, supplying the Torah's prohibition alongside the report of Moab's royal sacrifice.
Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.

english_plan.summary_english: Naaman travels to Israel seeking healing with his king's letter. He finally obeys Elisha's command to wash in the Jordan and is cleansed; Elisha refuses payment. Gehazi obtains gifts by lying, and Elisha declares that Naaman's disease will cling to him and his descendants.

english.note: The king sends a letter on Naaman's behalf so that Naaman may be healed; Naaman is not seeking a cure for the king. Elisha announces Gehazi's judgment, and the narrative then says Gehazi leaves with the skin disease. The Hebrew disease category is broader than modern Hansen's disease.

refs_template.english: Luke 4:27: Jesus names Naaman the Syrian as the one cleansed in Elisha's time, identifying the healing associated with Naaman's journey.
Leviticus 14:1-9: Priests examine a healed skin condition and administer cleansing rites, supplying the ritual context for the disease terminology used of Naaman.

english_plan.summary_english: Elisha sends a prophet to anoint Jehu as king of Israel with orders to destroy the house of Ahab; Jehu's army officers proclaim him king, he kills King Joram and chases down King Ahaziah, then orders eunuchs to throw Jezebel from a window in Jezreel where dogs consume her body.

english.note: Jehu calls to the people at the window and orders them to throw Jezebel down. The eunuchs carry out the order.

english_plan.summary_english: The Philistines rout Israel on Mount Gilboa, kill Saul's sons, and wound Saul, who falls on his own sword; they hang his head in the temple of Dagon. The men of Jabesh-gilead recover the bodies of Saul and his sons and bury their bones. Saul dies for his unfaithfulness, because he did not keep the word of the LORD and consulted a medium, so the LORD turns the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.

english.note: The displayed head and the recovered bodies are separate details. The men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve Saul's body and his sons' bodies, then bury their bones; the parallel in 1 Samuel places the bodies at Beth-shan.

refs_template.english: 1 Samuel 31:9-13: Saul's head is severed, his body is displayed at Beth-shan, and men of Jabesh recover his and his sons' bodies for burial.

english_plan.summary_english: Joab besieges and destroys Rabbah while David remains in Jerusalem. David then takes the Ammonite king's crown and plunder and puts the conquered people to forced labor. David's forces then fight several battles against the Philistines, with his men killing several giants including Lahmi the brother of Goliath.

english.note: Joab besieges Rabbah; David takes the crown and plunder and puts the people to work. The crown is said to weigh a talent of gold and to be placed on David's head. The passage does not explain how it was supported or say it was held above him. The English Berean Standard Bible renders 20:3 as forced labor with tools; other editions describe cutting the captives with those tools. This translation difference also affects the parallel in 2 Samuel 12:31.

refs_template.english: 2 Samuel 12:26-31: Joab takes Rabbah's water supply and summons David, who captures the city and takes its crown and plunder, distinguishing the stages of conquest.

english_plan.summary_english: Hiram completes the bronze furnishings for the temple - a large altar, the Sea with twelve bulls underneath, ten basins - and Solomon adds gold furnishings including the altar, lampstands, and doors. The total bronze work is so extensive that its weight cannot be calculated.

english.original: Hebrew: יָם מוּצָק (yam mutsaq), the cast sea
english.note: A single cast bronze basin, ten cubits across and five deep, about fifteen feet wide and seven and a half feet from brim to floor, standing on twelve bronze oxen in four groups of three facing out. Verse 6 says it was for the priests to wash in, the temple's replacement for the tabernacle's small bronze basin. This chapter gives its capacity as 3,000 baths (4:5), while 1 Kings 7:26 gives 2,000 baths. Using the Kings figure and an estimate of about 5.8 gallons per bath gives over eleven thousand gallons of water weighing more than forty tons; the two passages' stated figures remain distinct.
The ten lampstands are gold, and the sanctuary tables belong with the gold furnishings. They are not part of the bronze inventory.

refs_template.english: 1 Kings 7:48-50: The temple's altar, table, lampstands, and other sanctuary furnishings are described as gold, confirming their distinction from the bronze inventory.

english_plan.summary_english: Azariah prophesies to Asa that God will be with him if he seeks God, spurring Asa to remove idols and lead Judah and Benjamin in a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul. Asa deposes his grandmother Maakah for idolatry, brings dedicated treasures into the temple, and enjoys peace until the thirty-fifth year of his reign.

english.note: Verse 19 says there was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign. The next chapter records conflict with Baasha and a warning that Asa would have wars; the peace did not last for the rest of his reign.

refs_template.english: 2 Chronicles 16:1-9: Baasha threatens Judah and Hanani warns Asa of future wars, showing that the earlier period of peace did not last through his reign.

english_plan.summary_english: Josiah becomes king at eight, spends his youth destroying idols and high places throughout Judah and Israel, and in the eighteenth year of his reign sends officials to repair the temple; during repairs Hilkiah discovers the Book of the Law, and Josiah tears his robes in distress when he hears it read. The prophet Huldah tells Josiah disaster will come on Judah but because of his repentant heart he will not see the coming disaster, so Josiah gathers all the people and renews the covenant to follow the LORD.

english.note: The repairs begin in Josiah's eighteenth regnal year, about age twenty-six, and Shaphan reads the book to him. Huldah promises that he will be gathered to his grave in peace without seeing the coming disaster. The later account reports his death from battle wounds; the promise is not a description of an unwounded death.

refs_template.english: 2 Kings 22:3: The parallel account dates Josiah's commission to Shaphan to his eighteenth regnal year, confirming that the number describes his reign rather than his age.
2 Chronicles 35:20-24: Josiah is wounded in battle against Neco and dies in Jerusalem, supplying the later event to read beside Huldah's promise.

english_plan.summary_english: Enemies oppose the temple rebuilding from Cyrus to Darius. The chapter also recounts later accusations under Xerxes and Artaxerxes, including an order to halt rebuilding Jerusalem; verse 24 returns to the temple work halted until Darius's second year.

english.note: The chapter groups opposition from different reigns. The letters under Xerxes and Artaxerxes concern Jerusalem and its rebuilding; verse 24 returns to the earlier temple interruption under Darius. Artaxerxes' order is not the cause of an interruption that ended before his reign.

refs_template.english: Ezra 6:15: The temple is completed in Darius's sixth year, establishing its completion before the later Artaxerxes narrative.
Ezra 7:1: The narrative explicitly moves many years later to Artaxerxes' reign, distinguishing that setting from the temple's completion under Darius.
Nehemiah 2:1-8: Artaxerxes authorizes Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem and obtain timber for its gates and wall, supplying the later city-rebuilding setting.

english_plan.summary_english: Eliphaz implies that Job's suffering exposes wrongdoing, then describes a frightening night encounter with a spirit. In the account he reports, the spirit asks whether a mortal can be more righteous than God and stresses human frailty.

english.term: Who is speaking from here on
english.original: Hebrew: לֹא דִבַּרְתֶּם אֵלַי נְכוֹנָה (lo dibbartem elai nekhonah)
english.note: Eliphaz is reporting the spirit's words, not narrating a statement God has independently authenticated. This translation asks whether a mortal can be more righteous than God. The book introduces Job as upright and later records God's rebuke of Eliphaz and his friends.

refs_template.english: Job 42:7-8: The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for speaking inaccurately about Him and directs them to seek Job's intercession.
Job 1:1: The narrator introduces Job as blameless and upright, establishing the characterization against which Eliphaz's accusations must be read.

english_plan.summary_english: Job asks why the Almighty's judgment is not visible while the vulnerable are robbed, exploited, and killed. He describes wicked people acting under darkness, then their insecurity and death, challenging anyone to refute his account.

english.note: This remains Job's speech in a debate. His opening question and the statement that God charges no one with wrongdoing describe the apparent delay of justice. The later description of the wicked's end does not erase that protest or prove that every sufferer is being punished for personal wrongdoing.

refs_template.english: Job 21:7-16: Job protests that wicked people can enjoy long lives, secure homes, and prosperity, challenging a simple equation between present success and righteousness.
Job 42:7-8: The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for speaking inaccurately about Him and directs them to seek Job's intercession.

english_plan.summary_english: These wisdom sayings commend honesty, humility, generosity, and righteousness, contrasting their life-giving effects with the ruin caused by deceit and greed. They warn against trusting riches and praise those who refresh others.

english.note: These are wisdom sayings about righteous and wicked ways. They are not a promise that every faithful person will become wealthy or avoid suffering. Job and Ecclesiastes explicitly describe exceptions to a simple equation between present prosperity and righteousness.

refs_template.english: Job 21:7-16: Job protests that wicked people can enjoy long lives, secure homes, and prosperity, challenging a simple equation between present success and righteousness.
Ecclesiastes 7:15: The speaker observes a righteous person dying and a wicked person living long, supplying an explicit counterexample to guaranteed earthly safety.

english_plan.summary_english: The woman longs for open affection and declares love as strong as death, unquenchable and beyond purchase. The poem also asks what will be done for a little sister and records the woman's reply that she is a wall. The lovers close with an invitation to come swiftly.

english.original: Hebrew: בַּיּוֹם שֶׁיְּדֻבַּר־בָּהּ (ba-yom she-yedubbar bah, the day she is spoken for)
english.note: Verse 6 says love is as strong as death, not stronger. The speakers are not named in the Hebrew poem; verses 8-9 are commonly read as the brothers' words, with the woman replying in verse 10. They are not safely summarized as her plan to protect a younger sister.

refs_template.english: Genesis 29:18-20: Jacob's love for Rachel makes seven years of service seem like a few days, providing a narrative parallel for the strength of love.

english_plan.summary_english: Rezin of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah march against Jerusalem, and the LORD sends Isaiah to tell the trembling Ahaz that their plot will not stand; when Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, the Lord gives one anyway, the virgin conceiving and bearing a son called Immanuel, and before the boy knows to reject evil the land of the two dreaded kings will be laid waste, yet the LORD will also bring the king of Assyria on Judah, a hired razor that leaves the land to curds and honey, briers and thorns.

english.original: Hebrew: עַלְמָה (‘almah, ‘young woman’), Greek (LXX): παρθένος (parthenos), Aramaic: עַלִימְתָא
english.note: The Hebrew word almah is translated virgin here and young woman in some other versions. Isaiah 7:16 connects the sign with the crisis facing Ahaz; Matthew 1:22-23 applies the Greek wording to Jesus' virgin birth. The immediate setting and Matthew's application are both part of the biblical context.

refs_template.english: 2 Kings 16:5-9: Ahaz faces Rezin and Pekah's siege and appeals to Assyria for help, establishing the political crisis addressed by Isaiah's sign.
Matthew 1:22-23: Matthew presents Jesus' birth as fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy, supplying the New Testament application alongside Isaiah's setting under Ahaz.

english_plan.summary_english: Isaiah announces Moab's devastation, mourning, fleeing populations, and ruined water and vegetation. The oracle ends with a threat of further judgment, pictured as a lion against Moab's fugitives and survivors.

english.note: The first-person threat belongs to the prophetic announcement of judgment. The chapter does not depict Isaiah personally attacking Moab or bringing a lion against its refugees.

refs_template.english: Jeremiah 48:1-5: The LORD announces Moab's devastation and the mourning of its towns, providing a parallel divine oracle rather than an action personally inflicted by Isaiah.

english_plan.summary_english: The oracle calls for tribute to Zion and voices an appeal for shelter for Moab's fugitives. It anticipates a faithful ruler in David's house, then laments Moab's pride and ruined vineyards and announces that its glory will fade within three years.

english.note: In the wording used here, the appeal asks that Moab's fugitives receive refuge. English versions differ over the speakers and the relationship of Moab to the fugitives, so the summary needs to follow the displayed translation without reversing who seeks shelter.

refs_template.english: Jeremiah 48:29-33: The oracle condemns Moab's pride and laments ruined vineyards and lost harvest joy, paralleling Isaiah 16's judgment and mourning.

english_plan.summary_english: Isaiah announces judgment on Egypt's society, river, livelihoods, and leaders. He also pictures five cities turning to the LORD, an altar and boundary pillar as witnesses, and Egypt, Assyria, and Israel worshiping under God's blessing.

english.original: Hebrew: מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeaḥ) / מַצֵּבָה (matsebah); Greek (LXX): θυσιαστήριον / στήλη
english.note: Sign and witness to the LORD in Egypt (19:19-20). Verse 18 names five cities speaking Canaan's language. Verse 19 then describes one altar in Egypt's center and one pillar near its border, rather than a separate altar in every city.

refs_template.english: Zephaniah 3:9-10: God promises purified speech and worshipers bringing offerings from beyond Cush, paralleling the vision of nations turning to His worship.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD says Israel's sins, not a creditor's claim or lack of divine power, explain its estrangement, and He declares His power to redeem. The servant listens, endures abuse, and trusts God's vindication; those who fear the LORD are called to trust Him in darkness.

english.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר כְּרִיתוּת (sepher kerithuth, a document of cutting off)
english.note: Verse 1 does not simply deny that a separation occurred: it explicitly says the people were sold for their iniquities and their mother sent away for their transgressions. The questions about a certificate and creditors challenge the grounds and finality of the estrangement, while verse 2 asserts God's power to redeem.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 24:1-4: The law describes divorce certificates and prohibits a first husband reclaiming his former wife after another marriage, supplying the legal background to divorce language.
Isaiah 54:7-8: The LORD acknowledges briefly forsaking His people and promises compassionate return, supplying restoration context for Isaiah 50's separation language.
Jeremiah 3:8: The LORD describes giving faithless Israel a divorce certificate and sending her away, confirming that prophetic divorce imagery cannot simply be denied.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD esteems those who are humble and tremble at His word, and rejects worship joined to rebellion. He promises Jerusalem's restoration and the gathering of nations, while announcing judgment on the rebellious and comfort for His people.

english.note: The contrast is with worshipers who choose their own ways and delight in abominations. The chapter later still describes offerings, priests, and worship, so it does not simply say that every ritual offering is rejected.

refs_template.english: Malachi 1:6-14: Priests are rebuked for defective offerings while pure offerings are anticipated, distinguishing corrupt worship from a rejection of every offering.
Isaiah 1:11-17: The LORD rejects offerings joined to bloodshed and demands justice, identifying the rebellious conduct behind the condemnation of worship.

english_plan.summary_english: Judah's sin is pictured as engraved on its heart and altars. Jeremiah contrasts trust in people with trust in the LORD, prays for healing, and delivers a Sabbath warning: obedience brings continued life in the city, while refusal brings consuming fire.

english.note: The engraved writing pictures guilt deeply embedded in the people and their worship. It does not state that God cannot forgive or change them: verse 14 asks for healing, and Jeremiah 31 promises God's law written on the heart and sins forgiven.

refs_template.english: Jeremiah 31:31-34: The LORD promises a new covenant with law written on hearts and sins forgiven, providing context against reading engraved guilt as beyond forgiveness.
Ezekiel 36:26-27: The LORD promises a new heart and His Spirit enabling obedience, supplying the restoration counterpart to a deeply corrupted heart.

english_plan.summary_english: Jeremiah denounces royal injustice and announces disgrace and exile for Judah's kings. Jehoiachin is judged as a failed royal line: none of his offspring will prosper on David's throne in Judah.

english.note: The judgment concerns prosperity on David's throne in Judah. Zerubbabel, a later descendant, appears as governor rather than king, and Haggai calls him God's chosen signet. Matthew still includes Jeconiah in the genealogy; the passage cannot be reduced to a claim that he had no biological children.

refs_template.english: Matthew 1:11-12: Matthew includes Jeconiah, Shealtiel, and Zerubbabel in the genealogy, showing descendants continuing beyond the exile.
Haggai 1:1: Zerubbabel is identified as governor of Judah under Darius, establishing his office in the later setting alongside the judgment on Jehoiachin's royal line.
Haggai 2:23: The LORD calls Zerubbabel His chosen servant and likens him to a signet ring, supplying the later signet image alongside Jeremiah's rejection of Coniah.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD promises to gather and restore His people and make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, writing His law on their hearts and forgiving their sins. All His covenant people will know Him, and Jerusalem will be rebuilt and made holy.

english.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה (berith chadashah) - Greek: διαθήκη καινή (diatheke kaine)
english.note: The promise that all will know the LORD belongs to the new covenant announced with Israel and Judah. It is not phrased as a statement that every person already knows God regardless of that covenant. Hebrews quotes this promise in its account of Christ's covenant. Verses 31-34 are the only place in the Old Testament where the phrase new covenant appears.

refs_template.english: Hebrews 8:8-12: Hebrews quotes the covenant promise to Israel and Judah, including shared knowledge of the Lord and forgiveness, preserving the promise's covenant setting.
Hebrews 10:16-17: Hebrews repeats the promises of law on hearts and sins remembered no more, linking the heart-writing language with covenant forgiveness.

english_plan.summary_english: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that Jerusalem will burn and he will be taken to Babylon, though he will not die by the sword. God then condemns the people for freeing Hebrew slaves and taking them back, announcing judgment for the broken covenant.

english.note: Death in peace is set against death by the sword, not against captivity. The oracle says Zedekiah will be taken to Babylon; the later account says he was blinded and remained imprisoned until death. Verse 5 promises Zedekiah death in peace with the customary funeral fire and the lament Alas, lord.

refs_template.english: Jeremiah 39:6-7: Zedekiah sees his sons killed, is blinded, and is taken in chains toward Babylon, showing that the peace promise did not mean escape from capture.
Jeremiah 52:11: Zedekiah is taken to Babylon and kept in custody until death, specifying his captive end alongside the promise that he would not die by the sword.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD commands Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem's siege, lie on his sides for days assigned to Israel's and Judah's guilt, and eat measured food and water. After Ezekiel objects to human excrement as fuel, God permits cow dung; the sign depicts siege scarcity and exile defilement.

english.note: The 390 and 40 days are explained as days for years, but the chapter does not identify a calendar start and end for those years. It gives prophetic instructions and the exchange about fuel; further reconstructions of how the daily sign was performed remain interpretations.

refs_template.english: 2 Kings 25:1-4: Jerusalem endures a Babylonian siege and severe famine before its defenses are breached, supplying the historical siege context for Ezekiel's sign.
Numbers 14:34: Forty days of spying correspond to forty years of bearing guilt, supplying another explicit prophetic day-for-year reckoning.
Exodus 12:40: The text gives 430 years for Israel's stay in Egypt, supplying the numerical comparison made with Ezekiel's assigned days.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD orders the man in linen to scatter burning coals over Jerusalem; he receives the coals and goes out. The glory of the LORD moves from the temple threshold to the cherubim and the east gate as Ezekiel sees their faces and wheels.

english.note: Verse 2 commands scattering coals over the city, and verse 7 records the man receiving them and going out. The chapter does not separately describe the scattering. The vision signifies judgment as the LORD's glory departs; the later burning of Jerusalem is a related event, not another detail Ezekiel reports seeing here.

refs_template.english: Ezekiel 43:1-5: The LORD's glory returns through the east gate and fills the temple, reversing the departure described in Ezekiel 10.
2 Kings 25:9: The Babylonian destruction burns the temple, palace, and Jerusalem's major buildings, supplying the later historical fire associated with Ezekiel's judgment vision.

english_plan.summary_english: The man shows Ezekiel priests' rooms on the north and south sides of the temple courtyard where holy offerings will be stored and eaten; priests must change out of their ministry garments before leaving the holy area. He then measures the entire temple complex and finds it forms a perfect square, five hundred cubits on each side, with a wall separating the holy from the common.

english.note: This translation gives the enclosure as five hundred cubits on each side. Other versions render the measurement in reeds or rods, reflecting a textual and unit question. Ezekiel 40:5 defines a measuring reed as six long cubits, so the two renderings do not represent the same physical size.

refs_template.english: Ezekiel 40:5: The measuring rod is defined as six long cubits, establishing why a measurement in reeds or rods differs in scale from cubits.
Ezekiel 45:2: The sanctuary's section is described as five hundred cubits square with surrounding open land, providing a related dimension for comparison.
