english_plan.summary_english: The tribes receive their allotments from north to south. The central district has separate priestly land containing the sanctuary, Levitical land, and city land, with the prince's land beside it. The city's gates bear the tribes' names, and its name is The LORD Is There.

english.note: The sanctuary stands in the priestly allotment. The city and its common-use land form a separate strip within the larger district; the sanctuary is not placed inside the city. The chapter ends with the city's name, The LORD Is There.

refs_template.english: Revelation 21:12-13: The city has twelve gates named for Israel's tribes, three on each side, providing the later parallel to Ezekiel's tribal gates.
Ezekiel 45:1-6: The sanctuary stands within the priests' portion, with adjacent Levitical and city allocations, confirming the separation of sanctuary land and city land.

english_plan.summary_english: At the LORD's command, Hosea shows love again to an adulterous woman, paying silver and barley and requiring a period of sexual restraint. The sign depicts Israel's time without its institutions and its later return to the LORD and David its king.

english.original: Hebrew: וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי (va-ekkereha li, and I bought her for myself)
english.note: This translation identifies the woman as Hosea's wife again, commonly understood as Gomer, but the chapter does not repeat her name and other versions say a woman. Verse 2 gives fifteen shekels plus barley; comparing only the silver with the thirty-shekel payment in Exodus 21:32 does not establish the total value of the purchase.

english.term: What the buy-back price was worth
english.note: Verse 3:2 names fifteen shekels of silver plus a homer and a lethech of barley. Silver was weighed rather than counted; at roughly eleven grams per shekel, the silver alone is about six ounces. A homer is ten ephahs and a lethech is half a homer, so the grain amounts to one and a half homers. The text does not assign that barley a silver value, so the total cannot be identified as exactly half the thirty-shekel compensation in Exodus 21:32.

Barley was the cheap grain, poor man's bread and animal feed, harvested weeks before the wheat. The law prices a barley field accordingly (Leviticus 27:16), and the jealousy offering at Numbers 5:15 is barley flour with no oil and no incense on it, the plainest offering in the system. Barley forms part of the payment in 3:2, alongside fifteen shekels of silver.

refs_template.english: Exodus 21:32: Thirty shekels compensate the master of a servant gored by an ox, providing a legal comparison rather than a stated total value for Hosea's silver and barley.
Hosea 1:2-3: Hosea marries the specifically named Gomer after the LORD's command, supplying the earlier identification considered when reading the unnamed woman in chapter 3.

english_plan.summary_english: Edom's pride and defenses will fail because Esau's descendants betrayed their kin, the people of Judah, during Jerusalem's disaster. They gloated, looted, and intercepted fugitives. The Day of the LORD brings judgment, deliverance on Zion, and the LORD's kingdom.

english.original: Hebrew: אֱדוֹם (ʾEdom), עֵשָׂו (ʿEsav), שֵׂעִיר (Seʿir), Greek (LXX): Ἐδώμ, Ἠσαῦ, Σηείρ, Aramaic: אדום, עשו, שעיר
english.note: Esau and Jacob function here as ancestral names for Edom and Israel or Judah. The oracle is about later peoples and Jerusalem's disaster, not an account of the two patriarchs personally taking part in that event.

refs_template.english: Genesis 25:29-34: Esau exchanges his birthright for Jacob's red stew and is associated with the name Edom, supplying the ancestral background for Obadiah's national names.
Genesis 36:1-8: Esau is identified with Edom and settles his household in Seir, supplying the ancestral basis for the national names in Obadiah.
Numbers 20:14-21: Israel addresses Edom as a brother, but Edom refuses passage and threatens force, supplying an earlier example of conflict between the related peoples.
Psalm 137:7: The psalm recalls Edom urging Jerusalem's destruction, paralleling Obadiah's charge against the later nation rather than the patriarch personally.

english_plan.summary_english: Micah announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem for idolatry. Samaria's devastation is pictured as an incurable wound reaching Judah and Jerusalem, and Micah laments the towns facing disaster and exile.

english.note: The wound reaching Judah is part of the oracle's picture of devastation and judgment. The verse does not call it a contagious spread of Samaria's wickedness into Judah.

refs_template.english: 2 Kings 17:5-6: Assyria captures Samaria after a three-year siege and deports Israelites, supplying the destruction setting behind Micah's wound imagery.
2 Kings 18:13-17: Assyria captures Judah's fortified cities and sends a force to Jerusalem, paralleling Micah's image of devastation reaching Judah's gate.

english_plan.summary_english: Micah depicts corrupt rulers as butchers devouring the people and condemns prophets who promise peace for payment. Filled with the LORD's Spirit, he exposes injustice and announces that Zion and Jerusalem will be ruined despite the leaders' false confidence.

english.note: The skinning and cooking language portrays the rulers' predatory treatment of the people. The chapter identifies their concrete corruption as bribery, paid teaching, and paid prophecy; the imagery is not a separate historical report that those rulers literally ate their subjects.

refs_template.english: Jeremiah 26:18-19: Judah's elders quote Micah's warning about Jerusalem and recall Hezekiah seeking God, preserving the prophecy's later reception.
Ezekiel 22:27-29: Officials are likened to wolves while extortion and oppression are explicitly named, supplying a parallel for Micah's predatory imagery.

english_plan.summary_english: The LORD calls creation to hear His case and recalls His saving acts. A worshiper asks what offering could answer the charge, even imagining a firstborn; the answer is justice, mercy, and humble walking with God. The chapter then condemns fraudulent trade and the ways of Omri and Ahab.

english.original: Hebrew: בְּכוֹרִי (bekhori, my firstborn) - פְּרִי בִטְנִי (peri vitni, the fruit of my body)
english.note: The questions in verses 6-7 come from the one asking how to approach the LORD, not from God requesting ever larger sacrifices. The firstborn question is part of that escalating rhetoric; it is not a command to sacrifice a child. Verse 8 states the answer.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 12:31: Israel must not imitate the nations' worship that burns sons and daughters, providing the Torah's prohibition of child sacrifice.
1 Samuel 15:22: Samuel declares obedience better than sacrifice, supplying a parallel to Micah's answer about what the LORD requires.
Hosea 6:6: The LORD calls for mercy and knowledge of God above sacrifice, paralleling Micah's correction of an escalating focus on offerings.

english_plan.summary_english: Malachi condemns priests who corrupt their calling and men who betray their covenant wives. He calls the people to faithfulness in worship and marriage, warns against violence, and rebukes their claim that God approves evildoers or neglects justice.

english.original: Hebrew: וְכִסָּה חָמָס עַל־לְבוּשׁוֹ (v'chissah chamas al-levusho)
english.note: Spreading the edge of your garment over a woman was the gesture that claimed her as wife. Ruth asks Boaz for exactly that in Ruth 3:9, and Ezekiel 16:8 uses it of the LORD covering Israel and entering a covenant with her. Malachi says the same garment comes back covered in violence. The Hebrew of verse 16 is difficult. This translation reads God as saying He hates divorce; others refer to the man who hates and divorces his wife. Both readings occur in a passage condemning marital betrayal and violence. Other biblical discussions of divorce belong alongside this verse rather than being replaced by a slogan.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 24:1-4: The law describes divorce certificates and prohibits a first husband reclaiming his former wife after another marriage, supplying the legal background to divorce language.
Matthew 19:3-9: Jesus answers a divorce dispute by citing creation, explaining Moses' concession, and stating an exception for sexual immorality, supplying further marriage context.

1 Corinthians 7:10-15: Paul discusses separation, reconciliation, mixed-belief marriages, and an unbelieving spouse's departure, supplying the distinct circumstances addressed in later divorce teaching.

english_plan.summary_english: Jesus warns against judging others while ignoring one's own faults, since the same measure will be used in return, promises that everyone who asks receives, and sums up the Law and the Prophets in doing to others as you would have them do to you; he sets the narrow gate against the broad way, exposes false prophets by their fruit and empty 'Lord, Lord' claims, and ends with the houses built on rock and on sand.

english.original: Hebrew: שָׁפַט (shafat), Greek (NT): κρίνω (krinō, ‘judge/decide/condemn’), Aramaic: דן (dan)
english.note: The warning concerns judging others while ignoring one's own faults. Jesus says the measure used will be measured back, then tells the hearer to remove the beam first so that he can see clearly to help his brother (7:1-5).

refs_template.english: Luke 6:37-42: Jesus joins warnings against judging and condemning with forgiveness, then says to remove one's own beam before helping with a brother's speck, matching Matthew's warning against hypocrisy.
John 7:24: Jesus calls for judging justly rather than by appearances.

english_plan.summary_english: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured, Moses and Elijah appear, and the Father's voice commands the disciples to listen to him; coming down, Jesus identifies Elijah's coming with John the Baptist, frees a boy his little-faith disciples could not, saying mustard-seed faith moves mountains, again foretells his death and rising, and tells Peter to obtain a coin from a fish's mouth and use it to pay the temple tax for them both.

english.note: The stater is the four-drachma coin specified in Jesus' instruction to Peter, enough for two two-drachma payments (17:24-27). Matthew records the instruction and promise; he ends the scene without narrating the catch or payment.

refs_template.english: Exodus 30:13-16: The LORD requires a half-shekel offering from those counted, rich and poor alike, for sanctuary service, providing the Torah background to the temple-tax question.

english_plan.summary_english: Jesus grounds marriage in the Creator making them male and female, one flesh not to be separated, says that a man who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery, and blesses the little children; a rich young man goes away grieving rather than sell all and follow, so Jesus tells the astonished disciples that a camel passes a needle's eye easier than a rich man enters the kingdom, yet with God all things are possible, and promises thrones and a hundredfold to those who left everything.

english.note: The exception in 19:9 occurs in a sentence about divorce followed by marriage to another person. Verse 8 describes the Mosaic divorce provision as a concession to hardness of heart. Porneia is rendered here as sexual immorality; the summary follows this sentence rather than attempting a complete set of marriage rulings.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 24:1-4: Moses describes divorce and a woman's subsequent marriage, then forbids her first husband taking her back after that marriage; this is the certificate passage raised in Jesus' discussion.
1 Corinthians 7:10-16: Paul tells spouses not to separate and addresses a further situation: a believer should remain with a willing unbelieving spouse, but let an unbeliever who leaves depart.

english_plan.summary_english: In Jesus' parable, a landowner pays the eleventh-hour workers the same denarius as the first, for the last will be first; going up to Jerusalem, Jesus foretells his condemnation, crucifixion, and third-day rising, answers the request of Zebedee's sons by making service the way to greatness, since the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many, and opens the eyes of two blind men near Jericho.

english.note: Jesus introduces the vineyard workers as a comparison for the kingdom of heaven (20:1). The landowner and workers belong to that parable, whose closing saying concerns the last and the first (20:16).

refs_template.english: Luke 15:11-32: In Jesus' parable, a father welcomes his returning younger son and answers the older son's anger at the celebration, a comparison with resentment of the landowner's generosity.

english_plan.summary_english: In Jesus' parable, a king's wedding banquet fills with guests from the crossroads after the invited refuse, and a man without wedding clothes is cast out, for many are called but few are chosen; Jesus then answers his testers, giving to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, declares God the God of the living at the resurrection, names love of God and neighbor as the commandments carrying the Law, and silences the Pharisees by asking how David's son can be David's Lord.

english.note: Matthew explicitly introduces the wedding banquet as a parable about the kingdom of heaven (22:1-2). The king, the invited guests, and the man without wedding clothes are figures within that teaching story.

refs_template.english: Luke 14:16-24: Jesus tells a banquet parable in which invited guests make excuses and the host brings in poor and disabled people, then others from the roads, paralleling Matthew's refused invitations.

Zephaniah 1:7-8: The LORD's coming judgment is pictured as a sacrifice, and those dressed in foreign apparel are among those punished, providing a different prophetic setting for clothing imagery and judgment.

english_plan.summary_english: Jesus tells parables of ten virgins awaiting a bridegroom and servants entrusted with talents, calling for readiness and faithfulness. He then describes the Son of Man gathering the nations and separating people like sheep and goats according to their treatment of "the least of these brothers of Mine," ending with eternal punishment and eternal life.

english.note: The ten virgins and talents are teaching comparisons introduced in 25:1 and 25:14. In 25:31 Jesus turns to the coming of the Son of Man. Verse 40 calls those whose treatment matters 'these brothers of Mine'; the wording is preserved here without replacing that phrase with a narrower or broader identification.

refs_template.english: Matthew 24:42-44: Jesus tells his disciples to stay ready because the Son of Man will come at an unexpected hour, the warning developed in the bridegroom parable.
Matthew 10:40-42: Receiving Jesus' messengers is linked with receiving him.

english_plan.summary_english: Women find the stone rolled away and hear that the crucified Jesus has risen, with word for his disciples and Peter, and they flee trembling; the risen Lord then appears to Mary Magdalene, to two walkers, and to the Eleven, rebukes their unbelief, sends them into all the world to preach the gospel to every creature with signs following, and is taken up into heaven to sit at the right hand of God.

english.note: Verses 9-20 are commonly called Mark's longer ending. Some early manuscripts end after verse 8, and others contain a shorter ending, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. The longer ending is included in this edition; the manuscript variation concerns this ending rather than the empty-tomb report in verses 1-8.

refs_template.english: Matthew 28:16-20: The risen Jesus sends the Eleven to make disciples of all nations, baptize, and teach obedience, giving another Gospel's commission account alongside Mark's longer ending.
Luke 24:50-53: Jesus blesses his disciples near Bethany and is carried into heaven, giving Luke's account of the ascension also reported in Mark's longer ending.

english_plan.summary_english: John preaches repentance, answers the crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers, and points to one mightier who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends like a dove and a voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son; his genealogy runs through Joseph, David, and Abraham to Adam. Luke also reports Herod's imprisonment of John after John rebukes his conduct.

english.note: Luke closes his account of John's public ministry with the imprisonment report (3:19-20), then returns to Jesus' baptism (3:21-22). The placement of the report is not a statement that John was imprisoned before that baptism; Mark 1:9-14 gives the order explicitly.

refs_template.english: Mark 1:9-14: Jesus' baptism precedes John's arrest in Mark's sequence.
John 3:22-24: John is still baptizing before his imprisonment.

english_plan.summary_english: Jesus defends his grain-picking disciples as the Son of Man, Lord of the Sabbath, and restores a withered hand; after a night of prayer he chooses the twelve apostles, and on a level place he blesses the poor, pronounces woes on the rich, commands love of enemies and mercy like the Father's, warns against condemning others while ignoring one's own faults, says each tree is known by its fruit, and ends with the houses built on rock and on ground without foundation.

english.note: The command about judging stands beside commands not to condemn and to forgive (6:37). Jesus then warns against trying to remove another person's speck while ignoring one's own beam, and says to remove the beam first so one can see clearly to help (6:41-42).

refs_template.english: Matthew 7:1-5: Jesus says the measure used to judge will be used in return and tells the hearer to remove his own beam before helping with his brother's speck, matching Luke's warning against hypocrisy.
John 7:24: Jesus calls for judging justly rather than by appearances.

english_plan.summary_english: Supported by women he healed, Jesus tells the sower parable, explains the soils as ways of hearing the word, and calls those who hear and do God's word his mother and brothers; he stills a storm with a word, frees the Gerasene man from the demons called Legion, permitting them to enter pigs that then drown, heals the woman who touches his fringe after twelve years of bleeding, and raises Jairus's daughter with 'Child, get up!'

english.note: Legion is the name given because many demons had entered the man (8:30). The demons leave him and enter the pigs; the pigs then rush into the lake and drown, while the man is found clothed and in his right mind (8:33-35).

refs_template.english: Mark 5:9-15: Jesus permits the demons to enter the pigs; the pigs drown, while the man is later found clothed and in his right mind, clarifying the different actors and outcomes.

english_plan.summary_english: Jesus sends the Twelve to preach and heal, perplexing Herod, and feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish; Peter confesses him the Christ of God, Jesus foretells his suffering and calls for daily cross-bearing, is transfigured in glory speaking with Moses and Elijah of his departure at Jerusalem, frees a convulsing boy, again predicts his betrayal, sets a child as the measure of greatness, refuses fire on a Samaritan village, and warns that anyone who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is unfit for the kingdom of God.

english.note: The plow saying is Jesus' illustration of the commitment required to follow him (9:57-62). The picture is of someone beginning to plow and looking back; Jesus applies it to fitness for the kingdom.

refs_template.english: 1 Kings 19:19-21: Elisha leaves his plowing, asks to say goodbye to his parents, and then follows Elijah, connecting a prophetic call with both the farewell request and the plow image in Luke.

english_plan.summary_english: The seventy-two go out two by two and return rejoicing that demons submit, though Jesus points them to names written in heaven and blesses what they see; a law expert's test draws out love of God and neighbor, and Jesus answers his question with the story of a Samaritan showing mercy to a robbers' victim, and busy Martha hears that Mary, listening at the Lord's feet, has chosen the good portion.

english.note: Jesus tells the Samaritan story in response to the law expert's question, 'Who is my neighbor?' (10:29-30). At its end Jesus asks which person became a neighbor to the injured man, and the expert answers, 'The one who showed him mercy' (10:36-37).

refs_template.english: Isaiah 52:7: A messenger proclaims peace, good news, and salvation to Zion and announces that God reigns, a prophetic comparison for the messengers' proclamation in Luke.
Deuteronomy 6:5: The command to love the LORD with all one's heart, soul, and strength is one of the Torah texts the law expert quotes before Jesus tells the Samaritan story.
Leviticus 19:18: The command to love one's neighbor accompanies a ban on revenge and grudges; the law expert quotes it before asking Jesus to define neighbor.

english_plan.summary_english: Warning against the leaven of hypocrisy, Jesus commands fear of the One with authority over hell and promises the Spirit's words under trial; in his parable a rich man's plans for larger barns are cut short when his life is required that night, so he tells his little flock not to worry but to seek the kingdom, to keep lamps burning like servants awaiting their master, and to be faithful managers, then declares he brings fire and division rather than peace and chides hypocrites who read the sky but not the present time.

english.note: Luke introduces the rich man's account as a parable (12:16). His plans concern bigger barns, but God's warning concerns his life being required that night and the possessions passing to someone else (12:18-20). The point is stated in 12:21: storing treasure without being rich toward God.

refs_template.english: Ecclesiastes 2:18-21: The worker leaves accumulated goods to another.
Psalm 49:16-20: Wealth cannot be carried away at death.

english_plan.summary_english: Unless you repent you will all likewise perish, Jesus warns after Pilate's slaughter and Siloam's tower, then tells a parable in which a vineyard keeper asks for one more year to tend a barren fig tree; he frees a daughter of Abraham bound eighteen years on the Sabbath, likens the kingdom to mustard seed and leaven, commands striving through the narrow door before the master shuts it, answers Herod the fox with his third-day goal, and laments over Jerusalem, whose house is left desolate.

english.original: Hebrew: מָשָׁל (māšāl), Greek (NT): παραβολή (parabolή), Aramaic (Syriac): ܡܬܠܐ (mtlʾ)
english.note: The fig tree appears in a parable introduced in 13:6. Its keeper asks the owner for another year to dig around it and fertilize it (13:8-9). The owner gives no recorded answer, leaving the warning about fruit and repentance open.

refs_template.english: Isaiah 5:1-7: The LORD's vineyard is Israel: he expects justice but finds bloodshed and announces judgment, providing a prophetic comparison for Luke's fruitless-tree warning.

english_plan.summary_english: At a leading Pharisee's Sabbath table Jesus heals a man with dropsy, teaches guests to choose the last place since the self-exalting will be humbled, and tells hosts to invite the poor who cannot repay; in his parable, a great banquet fills with the poor and the compelled after the invited excuse themselves, and he turns to the crowds with the cost of discipleship, carrying one's cross, counting like the tower builder and the warring king, and giving up everything.

english.note: At the meal Jesus instructs guests to choose the lower place (14:7-11). He then tells the story of a great banquet whose original invitees refuse to attend (14:16-24). The seating counsel and banquet story are teachings within the account of the meal.

refs_template.english: Proverbs 25:6-7: The seating instruction echoes the counsel to wait to be invited higher.
Isaiah 25:6: The LORD prepares a feast for all peoples.

english_plan.summary_english: Answering grumbling over his welcome of sinners, Jesus tells parables of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine for one lost sheep and the woman who sweeps for one lost coin, for heaven rejoices over one repenting sinner; then a prodigal son returns from the far country to a father who runs to embrace him and feasts, telling the angry older brother that this brother of yours was dead and is alive again, lost and found.

english.note: The lost sheep, lost coin, and two sons form Jesus' parabolic answer to those criticizing his welcome of sinners (15:1-3). The recurring theme is joy over the lost being found; the final story also leaves the older son's response to the father's appeal unreported (15:28-32).

refs_template.english: Ezekiel 34:11-16: The LORD promises to search for his scattered flock, recover the strays, and strengthen the weak, providing a prophetic comparison for Jesus' lost-sheep parable.

english_plan.summary_english: Jesus tells two parables: a persistent widow and an unjust judge teach perseverance in prayer, while a tax collector asking for mercy goes home justified rather than a self-confident Pharisee; Jesus receives the little children as those to whom the kingdom belongs, watches a wealthy ruler balk at selling all, says what is impossible with man is possible with God, foretells his mocking, death, and third-day rising, and gives sight to a blind beggar near Jericho whose faith has healed him.

english.note: Both opening scenes are explicitly called parables (18:1,9). The unjust judge is used in a contrast with God's care for those who cry to him, and the second parable addresses people who trust in their own righteousness and despise others (18:7-9).

refs_template.english: Luke 11:5-13: Jesus uses a midnight request for bread to teach persistence, then describes the Father's giving of the Holy Spirit to those who ask, complementing the widow parable's call to prayer.

english_plan.summary_english: Salvation comes to the house of Zacchaeus, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost; Jesus tells a parable in which a nobleman entrusts minas to servants while subjects reject his rule, Jesus rides the colt down the Mount of Olives amid cries of 'Blessed is the King,' weeps over Jerusalem, whose enemies will leave no stone on another because it missed its visitation, and drives the sellers from the temple as the leaders seek to kill him.

english.note: Luke states why Jesus tells the minas parable: his listeners suppose that the kingdom will appear immediately because he is nearing Jerusalem (19:11). The nobleman, servants, and hostile subjects are figures in that story, which is distinct from the surrounding accounts of Zacchaeus and the entry into Jerusalem.

refs_template.english: Matthew 25:14-30: A master entrusts different amounts to servants and later judges their stewardship, a separate parable from Luke's account of ten servants given minas.

english_plan.summary_english: Satan enters Judas, who arranges the betrayal; at the Passover table Jesus gives the bread and the cup of the new covenant in his blood, names the betrayer's hand beside his, makes the leader like the one who serves, and tells sifted Simon to strengthen his brothers when he turns back. On the Mount of Olives an angel strengthens him as he prays in anguish, and his sweat falls like drops of blood; seized after the kiss, he is denied three times by Peter before the rooster crows, mocked and beaten, and tells the Sanhedrin that from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.

english.note: In 22:43 the angel strengthens Jesus; verse 44 then describes his earnest prayer and sweat like drops of blood. The comparison is the wording of the verse. Some manuscripts omit verses 43-44, a variation recorded in the Berean Standard Bible footnote.

refs_template.english: Matthew 26:36-46: Jesus prays for the cup to pass, submits to the Father's will, and calls the sleeping disciples to watch and pray, paralleling Luke's prayer scene.

Mark 14:32-42: Jesus prays in distress for the cup to be taken away while submitting to the Father's will, then repeatedly finds the disciples asleep, giving Mark's account of the prayer before his arrest.

english_plan.summary_english: When the woman's accusers withdraw one by one before 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone,' Jesus does not condemn her and tells her to sin no more; declaring himself the light of the world, he warns that those who disbelieve die in their sins, promises that the truth will set free those who continue in his word, tells his opponents that their father the devil is a liar and murderer, and declares 'before Abraham was born, I am,' so they pick up stones as he leaves the temple.

english.note: John 7:53-8:11 is included in this edition. Some early manuscripts do not contain this passage, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote at 7:52 records. Within the account, Jesus both refuses to condemn the woman and tells her to sin no more (8:10-11).

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 17:6-7: Witnesses are required and initiate the execution.
Leviticus 20:10: The law prescribes death for both the adulterer and the adulteress, while John's scene describes the accusers bringing only the woman.

english_plan.summary_english: Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly nard for his burial over Judas's protest, and crowds come to see Lazarus too; riding a young donkey into Jerusalem amid palm branches and Hosannas, after Greeks ask to see Jesus and Philip and Andrew relay the request, Jesus declares that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified, a grain of wheat must die to bear much fruit, and when lifted up he will draw everyone to himself, while Isaiah's words explain the unbelief and Jesus cries out that he came as light, speaking exactly what the Father commanded.

english.note: A costly perfume oil extracted from the Himalayan Nardostachys plant; imported across the Silk Road. John 12:3 describes Mary anointing Jesus' feet with a pound of pure nard, and Judas values the perfume at 300 denarii in 12:5. Mark 14:3 describes an unnamed woman breaking a flask and pouring perfume on Jesus' head.

Philip and Andrew bring the Greeks' request to Jesus; John records his response without describing the requested meeting (12:20-23). John names Mary and describes her anointing his feet and wiping them with her hair (12:3). Mark 14:3 describes an unnamed woman breaking a flask and pouring perfume on his head. Combining every detail as one event is a harmonization beyond John's narration.

refs_template.english: Mark 14:3-9: Mark records an unnamed woman breaking a flask and anointing Jesus' head.
Matthew 26:6-13: Matthew likewise describes an unnamed woman and anointing of the head.

english_plan.summary_english: In the garden Jesus' 'I am He' sends the arresting band to the ground, and Jesus tells Peter to sheath his sword, declaring his resolve to drink the cup the Father has given him; questioned by Annas and sent bound to Caiaphas while Peter denies him three times until the rooster crows, he then tells Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world and that he was born to testify to the truth, and the crowd chooses Barabbas over the King in whom Pilate finds no basis for a charge.

english.note: Jesus tells Peter to put the sword back in its sheath and declares that he will drink the Father's cup (18:11). John narrates questioning before Annas, who then sends Jesus bound to Caiaphas (18:19-24). Matthew and Mark supply a high-priestly hearing; that detail belongs to the parallel accounts.

refs_template.english: Matthew 26:57-68: Matthew names Caiaphas at the gathering where the high priest questions Jesus and the council condemns him, supplying the hearing details for comparison with John's account.
Mark 14:53-65: Mark places Jesus before the high priest and council, where witnesses disagree and Jesus is questioned about being the Christ, supplying another Gospel's account of the hearing.

english_plan.summary_english: Peter heals a man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate in the name of Jesus, and the man walks and leaps praising God; to the amazed crowd Peter declares that God glorified His servant Jesus, whom they killed but whom God raised from the dead, and calls them to repent so that times of refreshing may come.

english.note: Peter distinguishes the human action from God's action: the crowd killed Jesus, and God raised him (3:15). He also attributes the man's healing to Jesus' name and the faith that comes through him (3:12,16).

refs_template.english: Acts 2:23-24: Peter likewise distinguishes the human killing from God raising Jesus.

english_plan.summary_english: The Jerusalem council rejects requiring circumcision for Gentile salvation. Its letter asks Gentile believers to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, blood, meat from strangled animals, and sexual immorality; Judas and Silas deliver the decision with Paul and Barnabas.

english.note: The dispute begins with a demand that Gentiles be circumcised to be saved (15:1). The council's letter rejects that burden and names four requirements (15:28-29). Verse 21 mentions Moses being read in the synagogues; the text does not reduce the whole decision to a single stated purpose such as table fellowship.

refs_template.english: Leviticus 17:10-14: The law forbids Israelites and resident foreigners to eat blood and requires hunted animals to be drained, supplying Torah background for the council's restrictions on blood and strangled meat.
Leviticus 18:6-23: The law prohibits incest, adultery, and other sexual acts, providing Torah context for the council's prohibition of sexual immorality.
Acts 21:25: Jerusalem's leaders repeat that Gentile believers should abstain from idol food, blood, strangled meat, and sexual immorality, confirming the contents of the earlier council letter.

english_plan.summary_english: Disciples at Tyre urge Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem; later Agabus predicts his arrest, and his companions plead with him not to go, but Paul remains resolved and ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus; while he purifies himself at James's counsel, Jews from Asia incite the crowd, which beats him until Roman soldiers arrest him, and he gains leave to address the people.

english.note: Luke distinguishes the messages: the Tyre disciples tell Paul through the Spirit not to go (21:4), while Agabus predicts what will happen to him there (21:11). Paul continues despite his companions' pleas. In Acts 20:22-24, Paul also describes himself as compelled by the Spirit to go and says that the Holy Spirit warns him of imprisonment and hardships. These statements should be preserved without turning the summary into a verdict on Paul's obedience.

refs_template.english: Acts 20:22-24: Paul says the Spirit compels him toward Jerusalem while the Holy Spirit repeatedly warns of imprisonment and hardship; these statements provide the earlier setting for the warnings in Acts 21.

english_plan.summary_english: Paul describes believers groaning in their mortal bodies and longing to be clothed with life, with the Holy Spirit as God's pledge of what is to come; he urges them to live for Christ and serve as ambassadors of reconciliation, since Christ died for all and rose again.

english.note: Paul describes the body as an earthly tent and longs to be clothed with the heavenly dwelling. Verse 4 says he does not wish to be unclothed, but clothed so that mortality is swallowed up by life. His hope includes the transformation of mortal life.

refs_template.english: Romans 8:23: Believers await the redemption of the body.
1 Corinthians 15:53-54: The mortal puts on immortality.

english_plan.summary_english: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free, so believers must stand firm and not seek justification through circumcision, since what matters is faith expressing itself through love; called to serve one another in love, they are to walk by the Spirit, whose fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control stands against the obvious works of the flesh.

english.note: Paul's warning addresses seeking justification through circumcision and the law (5:2-4). He immediately says that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has value in Christ; what counts is faith expressing itself through love (5:6). Acts 16:3 records him circumcising Timothy in a different setting.

refs_template.english: Acts 16:3: Paul has Timothy circumcised because of the local Jews and Timothy's Greek father, a case to read alongside Galatians' warning about relying on circumcision for justification.
1 Corinthians 7:18-19: Paul counsels people not to change circumcision status.

english_plan.summary_english: United in one spirit, believers are to do nothing from selfish ambition but in humility take the mind of Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, emptied Himself, humbled Himself to death on a cross, and was exalted with the name above all names, every knee to bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord; they are to work out their salvation with fear and trembling as God works in them, shining as lights in the world, and Paul hopes to send Timothy of proven worth and is sending back Epaphroditus, who nearly died for the work of Christ.

english.note: Paul distinguishes the two travel plans. He hopes to send Timothy after learning how his own situation will turn out (2:19,23), while he considers it necessary to send Epaphroditus back to the congregation (2:25-28).

refs_template.english: Philippians 4:18: Epaphroditus is also named as the bearer of the Philippians' gift.

english_plan.summary_english: Paul warns that the day of the Lord has not yet come; the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness must come first. Paul describes a restrainer and says Jesus will destroy the lawless one at his coming.

english.note: Paul rejects the claim that the day has already come and names rebellion and the revealing of the lawless one (2:2-3). The Lord destroys that figure at the appearing of his coming (2:8). Paul refers to a restrainer but does not name the restrainer in this letter.

refs_template.english: Isaiah 11:4: The ruler slays the wicked with the breath of his lips, the image echoed when 2 Thessalonians describes Jesus destroying the lawless one.
Daniel 7:25-26: The one who opposes the Most High and oppresses the saints loses his dominion when the court convenes, a parallel to the lawless one's eventual defeat.

english_plan.summary_english: Paul instructs Timothy on how slaves should treat their masters, warns against false teachers who promote controversy and greed, and charges him to pursue righteousness while commanding the wealthy to be generous rather than arrogant. He emphasizes that godliness with contentment is gain, the love of money leads to ruin, and urges Timothy to guard the faith against false knowledge.

english.note: The instructions in 6:1-2 address enslaved believers and their conduct toward masters, including masters who are believers. Instructions addressed directly to masters appear in Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1.

refs_template.english: Ephesians 6:5-9: Paul instructs slaves to serve sincerely and masters to stop threatening, since both answer to the same heavenly Master; this passage directly addresses both groups.

Colossians 3:22-4:1: After telling slaves to serve Christ in their work, Paul tells masters to provide what is right and fair because they too have a heavenly Master; the instructions include both groups.

english_plan.summary_english: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, then appeals for Onesimus, whose father he became in chains; he sends him back and asks Philemon to welcome him as a beloved brother, receiving him as he would receive Paul himself, and pledges in his own hand to repay whatever Onesimus owes.

english.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother and as he would receive Paul himself (16-17). The letter refers to a period of separation and says, conditionally, 'if he has wronged you or owes you anything' (15,18). An escape, theft, and completed legal emancipation are not narrated. The familiar runaway-slave reconstruction is an inference.

Xenia is both the guest quarters and the bond itself. Guest-friendship in that world was a formal, binding, reciprocal obligation, not a courtesy: the host owed a guest food, lodging, and protection, and the tie passed down to the children of both houses. In the Iliad two warriors find mid-fight that their grandfathers were guest-friends, and they refuse to fight each other and swap armour instead (Iliad 6.212-231). Paul asks for a room in the house of the man he is asking to receive Onesimus as a brother.

refs_template.english: Colossians 4:9: Onesimus is called a faithful and beloved brother and one of the Colossians.

english_plan.summary_english: Believers must heed the salvation announced by Jesus and confirmed by witnesses, signs, and the Holy Spirit. Jesus shared human life and death, and God made the pioneer of salvation perfect through suffering. Through death he defeats the devil and frees those enslaved by fear of death, becoming a merciful and faithful high priest who helps those being tempted.

english.note: In 2:10 the one made perfect through suffering is the pioneer of salvation. The following verses explain his solidarity with those he saves and his merciful priesthood. Hebrews 4:15 describes him as without sin, so this perfecting is not presented as correction of previous sinful conduct.

refs_template.english: Hebrews 4:15: Jesus is described as tested yet without sin.
Hebrews 5:8-10: Jesus learns obedience through suffering and, made perfect, becomes the source of eternal salvation to those who obey him; God designates him high priest.

english_plan.summary_english: A high priest is chosen from among people to represent them before God; Christ did not claim this honor himself but was appointed by God and designated priest in the order of Melchizedek. In his earthly life he offered prayers and learned obedience through suffering. The author notes his readers have become dull and need basic instruction again rather than the deeper teaching they should be ready to receive.

english.note: God's call is the basis of Christ's priestly appointment (5:4-6). Verses 7-10 describe his prayers and the obedience learned through suffering. Hebrews 4:15 also says he was without sin; learned obedience does not mean he first had to stop disobeying.

refs_template.english: Numbers 16:1-40: Korah's company challenges the priestly order; the ground opens at the rebels' tents and swallows people and households, while fire consumes the 250 men offering incense.
Psalm 110:4: The LORD swears an unchanging oath appointing a priest forever in Melchizedek's order, the declaration Hebrews uses for Christ's priesthood.
Hebrews 2:10: The pioneer of salvation is perfected through suffering.

english_plan.summary_english: The author urges maturity and gives a solemn warning about falling away after the experiences described in verses 4-6, then expresses confidence in better things for the readers and urges persevering hope. God's promise and oath to Abraham ground that hope, with Jesus entering the heavenly sanctuary as high priest forever.

english.note: The warning names people who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, and tasted God's good word and the powers of the coming age, then fallen away (6:4-6). It describes their rejection in terms of crucifying the Son of God again and exposing him to public disgrace. Verse 9 nevertheless expresses confidence in better things for the readers. Interpreters differ over the spiritual status of those described and the force of the warning; the paragraph combines severe warning with a call to persevering hope.

refs_template.english: Hebrews 3:12-14: A related warning concerns unbelief and holding confidence to the end.
Hebrews 10:26-29: This warning names trampling the Son, profaning covenant blood, and insulting the Spirit of grace, giving the rejection language alongside the warning in Hebrews 6.

english_plan.summary_english: The author defines faith as confidence in unseen things and catalogs the faithful acts of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, and others who obeyed God without yet receiving all that God had promised. He notes that some faithful were tortured and killed while wandering destitute, yet all were commended for their faith.

english.note: Verse 33 says that some gained what was promised. Verses 39-40 speak of a promise whose completion joins them with later believers. The chapter holds particular fulfilled promises alongside that larger hope; it does not say that none of these people received any promised blessing.

refs_template.english: Genesis 21:1-3: Abraham and Sarah receive the promised Isaac.
Genesis 22:16-18: The LORD swears to multiply Abraham's descendants and bless all nations through his offspring, showing that the promises extend beyond the birth of Isaac.

english_plan.summary_english: John contrasts children of God, who love and practice righteousness, with children of the devil, who practice sin and hate their brothers; believers know love by Christ laying down his life.

english.note: This passage contrasts practiced righteousness and love with practiced sin and hatred (3:6-10,15). The same letter says that claiming to have no sin is self-deception and that believers who sin have an advocate in Jesus Christ (1:8-2:2). The contrast is not an instruction to deny believers' need for confession and forgiveness.

refs_template.english: 1 John 1:8-2:2: Believers confess sin and have Christ as their advocate.

english_plan.summary_english: John rejoices that the chosen lady's children walk in the truth and urges the commandment held from the beginning, to love one another by walking in His commandments; he warns that many deceivers who refuse to confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh have gone out, the deceiver and the antichrist, and warns against welcoming or greeting the deceiving teachers who arrive without this teaching, since doing so shares in their work.

english.term: Do not receive him into your home
english.note: The warning follows the description of deceivers who refuse the confession of Jesus Christ coming in the flesh (7-10). Receiving a visiting teacher into the household supplied lodging and support for his work; verse 11 warns that the welcome shares in that work. 3 John 1:5-8 gives the corresponding positive instruction about supporting faithful teachers.

refs_template.english: 3 John 1:5-8: Supporting faithful traveling teachers makes the hosts fellow workers in the truth.

english_plan.summary_english: Christ addresses three churches: Sardis is spiritually dead despite its reputation and must repent or face sudden judgment, though a few remain faithful; Philadelphia is weak but obedient and is promised keeping from the coming hour of testing; Laodicea is lukewarm and self-deceived about its poverty, and Christ calls it to buy spiritual refinement and repent.

english.note: The promise to Philadelphia concerns the coming 'hour of testing' (3:10), and the letter also calls for perseverance and holding fast (3:10-11). The verse does not name how this keeping will occur. It should not be expanded into a promise that this church will experience no further suffering.

refs_template.english: John 17:15: Jesus prays for his followers' protection without asking for their removal from the world.
Revelation 2:10: Christ warns Smyrna of imprisonment and ten days of tribulation, and calls the church to remain faithful even to death.

english_plan.summary_english: The first six seals reveal horsemen bringing conquest, war, famine, and death, martyrs crying for vindication, and cosmic upheaval as earth's rulers and peoples cry that the great day of wrath has come.

english.note: The martyrs still ask for vindication at the fifth seal (6:10), while those confronted by the sixth seal say the day of wrath has come (6:17). The fourth seal's sword, famine, plague, and beasts echo the judgments of Ezekiel 14:21. The visions should be summarized without placing every judgment after this chapter.

refs_template.english: Zechariah 6:1-8: Four chariots with differently colored horses go out to patrol the earth, providing a prophetic comparison for Revelation's mounted visions.
Joel 2:31: Joel describes the sun darkening and the moon becoming blood before the great day of the LORD, imagery also used when Revelation's sixth seal opens.
Ezekiel 14:21: The LORD names sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague as judgments against Jerusalem, the same four agents used by Revelation's fourth rider.

english_plan.summary_english: The seventh seal opens to silence; seven angels receive trumpets and an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the altar. As the first four angels sound their trumpets, devastating plagues strike the earth - hail and fire burn vegetation, something like a burning mountain is thrown into the sea, turning a third of it to blood, the star Wormwood contaminates water supplies, and darkness covers a third of the sky; an eagle warns of three more woes to come.

english.note: The second trumpet brings something like a burning mountain into the sea, and a third of the sea becomes blood (8:8-9). The third trumpet brings the star Wormwood onto rivers and springs, making their waters bitter (8:10-11). These are distinct visions.

refs_template.english: Jeremiah 9:15: The LORD threatens to give his people wormwood and poisoned water, a prophetic use of bitter, deadly drink echoed by the Wormwood star's effect on rivers and springs.
Exodus 7:20-21: When Aaron strikes the Nile as commanded, its water turns to blood and its fish die, the Exodus plague that parallels Revelation's sea-to-blood vision.

english_plan.summary_english: John sees a beast from the sea empowered by the dragon, blaspheming God and waging war against the saints. A second beast from the earth promotes worship of the first and requires a mark for buying and selling: the beast's name or the number of its name, given as 666.

english.note: Greek letters could serve as numerals, so 666 could be written as chi xi stigma. Some manuscripts instead read 616, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. Because every name was therefore also a sum, people played with it: a wall at Pompeii carries the line 'I love her whose number is 545'. That letter arithmetic is what 'let the one who has understanding calculate' refers to, and the text supplies the total rather than the name.

The second beast makes people worship the first and enforces the mark needed for buying and selling (13:12,16-17). The mark is described as the beast's name or the number of its name; verse 18 gives the number as 666. Some manuscripts read 616, as the Berean Standard Bible footnote records. The passage does not name a modern person or technology.

refs_template.english: Daniel 3:4-6: An image is worshiped under threat of death.
Revelation 14:9-12: Beast worship and its mark are contrasted with the saints' endurance.

english_plan.summary_english: Heaven erupts in praise as God judges the great prostitute, and a wedding supper for the Lamb is announced; then a rider on a white horse called Faithful and True wages war against the beast and kings of the earth, capturing the beast and false prophet while the beast's and kings' armies are defeated by the sword from the rider's mouth.

english.note: The armies of heaven follow the rider (19:14). The beast and the kings of the earth gather their armies to oppose him (19:19). Those opposing forces are defeated by the sword from the rider's mouth (19:20-21).

refs_template.english: Isaiah 11:4: The ruler strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth and slays the wicked with his breath, a prophetic comparison for the sword from the rider's mouth.
Ezekiel 39:17-20: The LORD summons birds and beasts to eat fallen warriors and drink their blood, the feast image echoed by Revelation's summons to birds and defeat of the rider's enemies.

english_plan.summary_english: The angel shows John the river of life, tree of life, and throne of God in the holy city where God's servants will serve him and see his face; Jesus declares he is coming soon, and the book closes with a warning against adding to or removing words from this prophecy.

english.note: The conclusion contains successive voices: Jesus speaks in 22:16, the Spirit and bride in 22:17, a first-person testimony in 22:18-19, and the response to Jesus' promise in 22:20. The warning belongs explicitly to the words of prophecy in this book; its speaker is not named again in verses 18-19.

refs_template.english: Deuteronomy 4:2: A parallel warning prohibits adding to or subtracting from the commanded word.
Deuteronomy 12:32: Israel is told to obey the commands without adding to or subtracting from them, a further parallel to Revelation's warning against changing the words of its prophecy.
